core.p: Visible light is the only part of the spectrum our eyes can detect. Its uses depend on that.
bullets: **Vision**: light reflected from objects enters our eyes and is focused on the retina.
**Photography**: a camera lens focuses light onto a sensor or film, which records the image.
**Illumination**: lamps, torches and lighting let us see in the dark.
Also used in optical fibres for endoscopes to see inside the body.

core.p: Ultraviolet has more energy than visible light. Some substances (fluorescent materials) **absorb UV and re-emit the energy as visible light**, which is the basis of most UV uses. UV also has enough energy to **kill microorganisms**.
bullets: **Security marking**: invisible ink that glows under a UV lamp marks valuables so they can be identified if stolen.
**Detecting forged bank notes**: real notes have marks that fluoresce under UV; forgeries usually do not.
**Fluorescent lamps**: UV is produced inside the tube, absorbed by the phosphor coating, which emits visible light. They are energy efficient.
**Disinfecting water**: UV kills bacteria and other microorganisms in water.
Also used in sunbeds to tan skin (with risks).

callouts.p: Absorbing ultraviolet radiation and then emitting visible light.

core.p: X-rays are highly penetrating. They **pass easily through less dense materials** such as soft tissue, but are **absorbed by dense materials** such as bone and metal. Detectors record where X-rays get through, producing a shadow picture.
bullets: **Medical X-rays**: show broken bones and dental problems; bones absorb X-rays and appear white, soft tissue lets them through and appears dark.
**Airport security scanners**: X-ray luggage to see metal objects such as weapons inside bags.
**Observing the internal structure of objects**: checking welds, cracks inside metal parts, or contents of packages without opening them.
CT scans use X-rays from many angles to build a 3D picture.

callouts.p: Mark schemes reward: bone absorbs X-rays, soft tissue transmits them.

core.p: Gamma rays have the **highest frequency and most energy**. They are very penetrating and **kill living cells**, including bacteria and cancer cells.
bullets: **Sterilising food**: gamma rays kill bacteria so food lasts longer; the food does not become radioactive.
**Sterilising medical equipment**: kills microorganisms on sealed packs of syringes and instruments, even through packaging, and works on items that heat would damage.
**Detection of cancer**: a gamma-emitting tracer is put into the body and detected outside with a gamma camera to show where it collects.
**Treatment of cancer (radiotherapy)**: focused beams of gamma rays kill cancer cells.

callouts.p: Irradiated food or equipment does not become radioactive. Gamma rays kill microbes and pass on.

core.h: Why each property suits each use
core.p: Grade 9 answers link the use to a property. Use this table to practise.
bullets: Signals: need to travel far and pass through the atmosphere or along fibres.
Heating: need to be absorbed by food (water for microwaves, surface for infrared).
Imaging inside: need to penetrate some materials but be absorbed by others.
Killing microbes: need high energy (UV, gamma).

head: Use
Radiation
Property it relies on
rows: Absorbed by bone, pass through tissue
High energy, penetrates packaging, kills microbes

core.p: Higher-frequency uses (UV, X-rays, gamma) carry risks because these radiations are ionising. Uses are justified when the benefit outweighs a controlled, small dose.
bullets: Medical X-rays: benefit of diagnosis outweighs small risk; staff use lead screens.
Radiotherapy: aims beams at the tumour from different angles to reduce damage to healthy tissue.
UV disinfection and sterilisation are done in sealed or shielded equipment.

callouts.p: If asked to explain a use, give the property AND what it achieves, e.g. 'gamma rays kill bacteria, so the food lasts longer'.

analogy.p: Think of the EM spectrum as a toolbox of torches that all shine at the same speed but differ in 'strength'. The gentle radio torch shines through walls and round corners, so it is used to send messages far away. The infrared torch is a warm glow that every warm object gives off, so a special camera can see people in the dark. The powerful gamma torch can burn through packaging and kill germs. You pick the torch whose beam does the job. The analogy breaks down because a real torch only gives visible light, and the 'strength' really means frequency and energy per photon, not brightness: a very bright radio transmitter still cannot sterilise anything.

terms.d: Transmitting radio or TV signals from one transmitter to many receivers.
Sending signals to and from satellites in orbit, using microwaves or high-frequency radio waves that pass through the atmosphere.
Sending information, such as phone calls or data, using EM waves.
Producing an image from the infrared radiation emitted by objects, showing differences in temperature.
A thin glass fibre that carries infrared or light signals by total internal reflection.
Complete reflection of a wave at a boundary inside a denser medium when the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle.
A device that sends coded pulses of infrared to control a television.
Providing visible light so that objects can be seen.
Absorbing ultraviolet and emitting visible light.
Marking property with ink that is only visible under ultraviolet light.
Using ultraviolet to kill bacteria and other microorganisms in water.
Killing all bacteria and other microorganisms on food or equipment, e.g. using gamma rays.
Using gamma rays (or X-rays) to kill cancer cells.
A gamma-emitting substance put into the body so that its location can be detected from outside, e.g. to detect cancer.
Able to pass through materials; X-rays and gamma rays are highly penetrating.

mistakes.w: Microwaves cook food by heating it from the outside like a grill.
mistakes.r: Microwaves **penetrate** into food and are **absorbed by water molecules**; infrared (grills) heats the surface.

mistakes.w: TV remotes use radio waves.
mistakes.r: Television remote controls use **infrared**.

mistakes.w: Satellites use radio waves because they reflect off the ionosphere.
mistakes.r: Satellites use **microwaves** because they **pass through the atmosphere**; reflection off the ionosphere would stop them reaching space.

mistakes.w: Bones show up on X-rays because X-rays pass through them.
mistakes.r: Bones **absorb** X-rays (appear white); soft tissue lets X-rays pass through.

mistakes.w: Gamma-sterilised food is radioactive.
mistakes.r: Food exposed to gamma rays does **not** become radioactive; the gamma rays kill bacteria.

mistakes.w: Forged notes are detected using X-rays.
mistakes.r: Forged bank notes are detected with **ultraviolet**: real notes have marks that fluoresce.

mistakes.w: Thermal imaging cameras see heat from cold objects.
mistakes.r: They detect **infrared emitted**; hotter objects emit more infrared so appear brighter.

mistakes.w: Optical fibres carry signals by refraction.
mistakes.r: Optical fibres carry signals by **total internal reflection**.

mistakes.w: UV is used in fluorescent lamps because it is visible.
mistakes.r: UV is **absorbed by the coating**, which then **emits visible light**.

exam.q: Name the type of electromagnetic radiation used in television remote controls.
model: Infrared.
exam.tip: Common 1-mark recall.

exam.q: Which type of electromagnetic radiation is used to sterilise medical equipment?
model: Gamma rays.
exam.tip: Sterilise = gamma.

exam.q: Give one use of ultraviolet radiation.
model: Any one of: security marking / fluorescent lamps / detecting forged bank notes / disinfecting water.
exam.tip: Stick to the spec list.

exam.q: Give two uses of microwaves.
model: Cooking.
Communications / mobile phones / satellite transmissions.
exam.tip: Two different uses, not two types of communication.

exam.q: Explain why microwaves are used to communicate with satellites.
model: Microwaves can pass through the atmosphere.
So they can reach the satellite in space (and return).
exam.tip: The key property is passing through the atmosphere.

exam.q: Explain how thermal imaging cameras can be used to find people trapped in a collapsed building.
model: People are warmer than their surroundings so emit more infrared.
The camera detects infrared and shows the warmer body as a different colour / brighter.
exam.tip: Mention that hotter objects emit more infrared.

exam.q: Explain why X-rays can be used to produce images of broken bones.
model: X-rays pass through soft tissue / flesh.
X-rays are absorbed by bone, so bone shows up (white) on the detector.
exam.tip: Need both transmission and absorption.

exam.q: Explain how ultraviolet is used to detect forged bank notes.
model: Real notes have special ink / marks that fluoresce (glow) under UV.
Forged notes do not show these marks under UV.
exam.tip: Use the word fluoresce.

exam.q: Gamma rays are used to treat food. Explain why, and why the food is safe to eat.
model: Gamma rays have high energy / are ionising.
They kill bacteria / microorganisms in the food.
So the food lasts longer / is safer.
The food does not become radioactive.
exam.tip: Address both parts of the question.

exam.q: Describe how gamma rays are used in the detection and treatment of cancer.
model: Detection: a gamma-emitting tracer is put into the body.
Gamma rays pass out of the body and are detected by a camera to show where the tracer collects / location of tumour.
Treatment: a beam of gamma rays is directed at the tumour.
Gamma rays kill the cancer cells (beam aimed from different angles to reduce damage to healthy cells).
exam.tip: Detection uses penetration; treatment uses cell killing.

exam.q: Describe uses of electromagnetic radiation in the home and explain which properties make each type suitable.
model: Microwaves cook food: absorbed by water molecules in food and penetrate into it.
Infrared in grills / toasters: absorbed by surface of food, heating it.
Infrared in TV remote controls: pulses carry coded signals over short range.
Visible light for illumination / vision / photography: detected by our eyes or camera.
Radio waves for broadcasting radio / TV: travel long distances, received by aerial.
Microwaves for wifi / mobile phones / satellite TV: pass through atmosphere to satellites.
exam.tip: For each use: name the radiation, the use, and the property. Aim for at least four linked uses.

worked.q: A hospital needs to (a) check a patient's broken arm, (b) sterilise sealed packs of syringes, and (c) send patient records quickly to another hospital. Choose a suitable EM radiation for each and justify your choice.
steps: (a) X-rays: they pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone, so the bone shows on the image.
(b) Gamma rays: very penetrating so pass through the sealed packaging, and high energy so they kill microorganisms; no heat that could melt plastic.
(c) Infrared in optical fibres: pulses travel by total internal reflection with little loss, carrying lots of data quickly.
worked.ans: (a) X-rays, (b) gamma rays, (c) infrared through optical fibres, each justified by its property.

worked.q: Explain why fluorescent lamps and security marking both rely on ultraviolet radiation.
steps: Both use substances that absorb UV and re-emit the energy as visible light (fluorescence).
Fluorescent lamp: UV produced inside the tube is absorbed by the coating on the glass, which emits visible light to illuminate the room.
Security marking: special ink is invisible in normal light but glows when a UV lamp shines on it, revealing the owner's mark.
worked.ans: Both depend on fluorescence: a material absorbs ultraviolet and emits visible light.

phy_edx.4.11.summary: Radio waves can be **produced by oscillations in electrical circuits**: an alternating current in a transmitting aerial makes electrons oscillate and emit radio waves of the same frequency. (Higher tier) When radio waves are **absorbed by a receiving aerial they may create an alternating current with the same frequency as the radio wave itself**, which is how radios and TVs pick up signals. More generally, **changes in atoms and nuclei** can both **generate** EM radiation over a wide frequency range and **be caused by absorbing** a range of radiations, from visible light emitted by electrons changing energy level to gamma rays from unstable nuclei.

core.p: An **alternating current (AC)** is a current that keeps reversing direction. In a transmitter, an electrical circuit makes charges (electrons) **oscillate** up and down a metal aerial. Oscillating charges produce an oscillating electric and magnetic field that travels away as a **radio wave**.
bullets: Radio waves **can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits**.
The circuit (oscillator) supplies an AC to the transmitting aerial.
Electrons in the aerial oscillate back and forth at the frequency of the AC.
The **frequency of the radio wave equals the frequency of the oscillation** in the circuit.
Radio frequencies are very high: from about 3 x 10^3 Hz (kHz) to about 3 x 10^9 Hz (GHz).

callouts.p: Radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits.

core.p: When radio waves reach a metal receiving aerial, they are **absorbed** and transfer energy to the free electrons in the metal. The oscillating field of the wave makes the electrons oscillate, so **an alternating current is created with the same frequency as the radio wave itself**.
bullets: Radio wave absorbed by aerial -> electrons in the aerial oscillate.
Oscillating electrons = **alternating current** in the receiver circuit.
The AC has the **same frequency** as the radio wave (and so as the original transmitter AC).
The receiver circuit decodes this AC to recover the sound or picture information.
This is the reverse of transmission: transmitter turns AC into waves, receiver turns waves back into AC.

callouts.p: When radio waves are absorbed they may create an alternating current with the same frequency as the radio wave itself.

core.p: The two ends of a radio link are mirror images of each other.
bullets: Both use a conducting aerial (metal rod or wire).
The frequency is the same throughout the whole chain.
Only a tiny fraction of the transmitted energy reaches any one receiver, so the received AC is very small and must be amplified.

callouts.p: The induced current has the SAME frequency as the radio wave, not the same size as the transmitter current.

core.h: Using the wave equation with radio waves
core.p: All EM waves, including radio waves, travel at 3 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum (and almost the same in air). Knowing the frequency of the oscillating circuit, you can find the wavelength using **wave speed = frequency x wavelength**, v = f x lambda.
bullets: v in m/s, f in Hz, wavelength in m.
Rearranged: wavelength = v / f and f = v / wavelength.
Watch prefixes: 1 kHz = 10^3 Hz, 1 MHz = 10^6 Hz, 1 GHz = 10^9 Hz.
Higher oscillation frequency -> shorter radio wavelength.

callouts.p: Convert MHz to Hz before using the equation, e.g. 100 MHz = 1.0 x 10^8 Hz.

core.h: Changes in atoms: electrons and energy levels
core.p: Electrons in an atom can only exist at certain **energy levels**. If an electron **absorbs** EM radiation of the right energy, it moves **up** to a higher energy level (the atom is **excited**). When it falls **back down**, it **emits** EM radiation.
bullets: Absorption: electron gains energy and moves to a higher level (further from the nucleus).
Emission: electron drops to a lower level and gives out EM radiation.
The bigger the energy drop, the **higher the frequency** of the radiation emitted.
Electron transitions typically produce **infrared, visible light and ultraviolet**; inner-electron changes in heavy atoms can produce **X-rays**.
If enough energy is absorbed, the electron can leave the atom altogether: **ionisation**.

callouts.p: Changes in atoms and nuclei can (a) generate radiations over a wide frequency range and (b) be caused by absorption of a range of radiations.

core.p: The nucleus also has energy levels. After radioactive decay (for example alpha or beta), a nucleus is often left with **excess energy**. It loses this by emitting a **gamma ray**, a very high-frequency EM wave.
bullets: Gamma emission comes from changes **in the nucleus**, not the electrons.
Nuclear energy changes are much bigger than electron energy changes, so gamma rays have the **highest frequencies**.
After gamma emission the nucleus has the **same number of protons and neutrons**, but less energy.
Nuclei can also absorb high-energy gamma radiation, which can change the nucleus.

core.h: A wide frequency range of radiations
core.p: Because the energy changes in atoms and nuclei vary hugely in size, the radiation they produce covers a **wide frequency range**.
bullets: Small energy changes (outer electrons, vibrations of molecules) -> infrared.
Medium energy changes (outer electrons) -> visible light and ultraviolet.
Large energy changes (inner electrons in heavy atoms) -> X-rays.
Very large energy changes (nucleus) -> gamma rays.
Radio waves are usually produced by oscillating charges in circuits rather than by single atoms.

core.p: The process also works in reverse: absorbing radiation **causes changes** in atoms and nuclei.
bullets: Absorbing visible or UV light can excite electrons to higher levels.
Absorbing UV, X-rays or gamma can ionise atoms by removing electrons completely.
Absorbing radio waves makes electrons in an aerial oscillate (creating AC).
This is why EM radiation can be detected: absorption produces a measurable change.

callouts.p: Ionisation from absorbing high-frequency radiation is the change that damages DNA in cells.

core.p: Real examples help in explain questions.
bullets: Fluorescent lamps: excited atoms emit UV, which is absorbed by the coating and re-emitted as visible light.
Flame tests and street lamps: excited electrons emit light of particular colours.
X-ray tubes: fast electrons hit a metal target, causing changes in the atoms that emit X-rays.
Radioactive tracers: nuclei emit gamma rays that are detected outside the body.
Radio and TV: oscillating circuits transmit; aerials absorb and produce AC.

core.p: Across all of these, the **energy change** decides the **frequency** of radiation emitted or absorbed. Bigger energy change, higher frequency.
bullets: Emission: energy lost by atom or nucleus is carried away by the EM radiation.
Absorption: energy of the radiation is gained by the atom or nucleus.
Energy is conserved in both processes.

callouts.p: Gamma rays come from the nucleus. Visible light comes from electrons changing energy levels. Do not mix them up.

analogy.t: Jumping on a trampoline and a ladder
analogy.p: A radio transmitter is like someone bouncing on one end of a long trampoline at a steady rate: the ripples travel across and make a person at the far end bounce at exactly the same rate (the receiver AC has the same frequency). An electron in an atom is like a person on a ladder: it can only stand on particular rungs. Lifting it up a rung needs energy put in (absorption); jumping down a rung releases energy (emission), and a bigger drop releases more energy (higher frequency). The trampoline breaks down because radio waves need no material to travel through; the ladder breaks down because electrons are not really little people climbing, and the rungs are not evenly spaced.

terms.d: A current that repeatedly reverses direction.
A repeated back-and-forth motion, such as electrons moving to and fro in an aerial.
An electrical circuit that produces an alternating current at a particular frequency to drive a transmitter.
A metal conductor that emits radio waves when AC flows in it, or absorbs radio waves to produce AC.
Equipment that turns an alternating current into radio waves.
Equipment that absorbs radio waves and turns them into an alternating current of the same frequency.
The number of oscillations or waves per second, in hertz (Hz).
wave speed = frequency x wavelength (v = f x lambda).
One of the fixed energies an electron in an atom (or a nucleus) can have.
An atom in which an electron has absorbed energy and moved to a higher energy level.
Giving out EM radiation when an electron falls to a lower energy level or a nucleus loses energy.
Taking in EM radiation, which transfers energy and causes a change in an atom, nucleus or aerial.
Removal of an electron from an atom, forming an ion, when enough energy is absorbed.
High-frequency EM radiation emitted when a nucleus loses excess energy.
The lowest energy level of an electron in an atom.

mistakes.w: Radio waves are produced by radioactive atoms.
mistakes.r: Radio waves are produced by **oscillations in electrical circuits** (AC in an aerial).

mistakes.w: The receiver produces a direct current.
mistakes.r: Absorbed radio waves create an **alternating current**.

mistakes.w: The current in the receiver has a different frequency from the radio wave.
mistakes.r: It has the **same frequency as the radio wave itself**.

mistakes.w: Gamma rays are emitted when electrons change energy level.
mistakes.r: Gamma rays come from changes **in the nucleus**.

mistakes.w: An electron emits radiation when it moves up an energy level.
mistakes.r: It **absorbs** radiation to move up; it **emits** radiation when it falls down.

mistakes.w: Atoms only give out one type of radiation.
mistakes.r: Changes in atoms and nuclei generate radiation **over a wide frequency range**.

mistakes.w: Gamma emission changes the number of protons.
mistakes.r: Gamma emission **does not change** the numbers of protons or neutrons; it only removes energy.

mistakes.w: Using 100 MHz directly in v = f x lambda gives a wavelength of 3 x 10^6 m.
mistakes.r: Convert to Hz first: 100 MHz = 1 x 10^8 Hz, so wavelength = 3 m.

exam.q: State how radio waves can be produced.
model: By oscillations (of charges / electrons) in electrical circuits / AC in an aerial.
exam.tip: Use 'oscillations in electrical circuits'.

exam.q: State what is produced in a receiving aerial when it absorbs radio waves. (Higher)
model: An alternating current.
exam.tip: Must say alternating.

exam.q: Describe how the frequency of the current in a receiver compares with the frequency of the radio wave. (Higher)
model: It is the same (frequency).
exam.tip: Simple recall.

exam.q: Name the part of an atom where gamma rays are produced.
model: The nucleus.
exam.tip: Not the electrons.

exam.q: Describe how a radio transmitter produces radio waves.
model: An (oscillating) circuit produces an alternating current in the aerial.
Electrons oscillate in the aerial and emit radio waves (of the same frequency).
exam.tip: Two linked steps: AC, then oscillating electrons emit waves.

exam.q: Explain how a radio receiver detects radio waves. (Higher)
model: The radio waves are absorbed by the aerial / make electrons in the aerial oscillate.
This creates an alternating current with the same frequency as the radio wave.
exam.tip: Mention absorption and same frequency.

exam.q: A transmitter oscillates at 2.0 x 10^8 Hz. Calculate the wavelength of the radio waves. Speed of EM waves = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s.
model: wavelength = v / f = 3.0 x 10^8 / 2.0 x 10^8
exam.tip: Rearrange first, then substitute; give the unit.

exam.q: Describe how an atom can absorb and emit electromagnetic radiation.
model: Electrons occupy energy levels.
An electron absorbs radiation and moves to a higher energy level.
The electron falls back to a lower energy level.
It emits electromagnetic radiation (frequency depends on the energy change).
exam.tip: Use 'energy level' and both 'absorb' and 'emit'.

exam.q: Changes in atoms and nuclei can generate radiation over a wide frequency range. Explain why different changes produce different types of electromagnetic radiation.
model: Different changes involve different amounts of energy.
A larger energy change produces higher frequency radiation.
Electron changes in atoms produce infrared / visible / UV (or X-rays for inner electrons).
Changes in the nucleus involve much more energy and produce gamma rays.
exam.tip: Link energy change to frequency, then give examples.

exam.q: Explain how radio waves are used to carry a signal from a transmitter to a receiver, and how changes in atoms and nuclei can also both produce and absorb electromagnetic radiation. (Higher)
model: An oscillating circuit produces AC in the transmitting aerial.
Oscillating electrons emit radio waves of the same frequency as the AC.
The receiving aerial absorbs the radio waves, creating an AC of the same frequency as the wave.
Electrons in atoms absorb radiation and move to higher energy levels; they emit radiation when they fall back.
Nuclei with excess energy emit gamma rays.
Different sized energy changes give radiation over a wide frequency range; absorption of radiation can cause these changes (e.g. ionisation).
exam.tip: Split the answer into two clear parts: circuits and aerials, then atoms and nuclei.

worked.q: A local radio station broadcasts at 97.4 MHz. Calculate the wavelength of its radio waves. (Speed of EM waves = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s.)
steps: Convert: 97.4 MHz = 97.4 x 10^6 Hz = 9.74 x 10^7 Hz.
Equation: v = f x wavelength, so wavelength = v / f.
wavelength = 3.0 x 10^8 / 9.74 x 10^7
wavelength = 3.08 m
worked.ans: About 3.1 m. The receiver aerial produces an AC at 97.4 MHz, the same frequency as the wave.

worked.q: The oscillator in a transmitter is changed so it oscillates at twice the frequency. Describe and explain what happens to the radio waves and to the current in a receiver tuned to them.
steps: The radio waves have the same frequency as the oscillations, so their frequency doubles.
The speed of the waves is unchanged (3 x 10^8 m/s), so from v = f x wavelength the wavelength halves.
When absorbed, the waves create an AC with the same frequency as the wave, so the receiver current also has double the original frequency.
worked.ans: Wave frequency doubles, wavelength halves, and the induced alternating current in the receiver also doubles in frequency.

phy_edx.4.3.summary: All electromagnetic (EM) waves are **transverse**: the electric and magnetic fields oscillate at right angles to the direction the wave travels and transfers energy. Every EM wave, from radio waves to gamma rays, travels at the **same speed in a vacuum**, 3 x 10^8 m/s, so they differ only in wavelength and frequency. All EM waves **transfer energy from a source to an observer** without needing a medium, which is why sunlight can warm the Earth across empty space and a microwave oven can heat food.

core.h: What the spec asks you to know
core.p: Spec points 5.7 and 5.8 are short but examined often, usually as 1 to 3 mark recall questions or as part of a longer question about the EM spectrum.
bullets: 5.7: **recall** that all electromagnetic waves are **transverse**.
5.7: **recall** that all EM waves travel at the **same speed in a vacuum**.
5.8: **explain, with examples**, that all EM waves **transfer energy from source to observer**.
These ideas link to the wave equation v = f x wavelength from Topic 4 (Waves).
Paper 1 content; both Foundation and Higher tiers, combined and separate science.

callouts.p: EM waves are transverse; they all travel at the same speed (3 x 10^8 m/s) in a vacuum; they all transfer energy from source to observer.

core.p: A transverse wave is one where the **oscillations are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer** (the direction of wave travel). Compare this with longitudinal waves such as sound, where the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
bullets: Transverse examples: all EM waves, ripples on water, waves on a string, S-waves (seismic).
Longitudinal examples: sound waves, P-waves (seismic).
Transverse waves have **peaks (crests) and troughs**; longitudinal waves have **compressions and rarefactions**.
Waves transfer **energy and information** but **not matter**: the medium (if there is one) oscillates about a fixed position and does not travel with the wave.

callouts.p: A wave in which the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.

core.h: What is actually oscillating in an EM wave?
core.p: Unlike a water wave, an EM wave has no particles moving up and down. It is made of **oscillating electric and magnetic fields**, which are at right angles to each other and both at right angles to the direction of travel. That is why it is transverse, and why it does not need a medium.
bullets: The changing electric field creates a changing magnetic field, which creates a changing electric field, and so on: the wave keeps itself going.
Because no particles are needed, EM waves can travel through a **vacuum** (empty space).
Sound cannot travel through a vacuum because it needs particles to pass on the vibrations.
At GCSE you only need to say the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer; mentioning electric and magnetic fields is extra depth.

callouts.p: If a question asks why we can see the Sun but not hear it, say: light is an EM wave so can travel through a vacuum; sound needs a medium (particles) to travel.

core.p: All EM waves travel at exactly the same speed in a vacuum, about **300 000 000 m/s (3 x 10^8 m/s)**. This is often called the **speed of light**, but it applies equally to radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.
bullets: Speed in a vacuum = 3 x 10^8 m/s (300 000 km/s).
In air the speed is very slightly less, so it is usually taken as 3 x 10^8 m/s as well.
In denser materials such as glass or water EM waves slow down (this causes refraction, covered in 5.13-5.14).
Light from the Sun (150 million km away) takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.
Gamma rays from a distant star and radio waves from the same star arrive at the same time, because they travel at the same speed.

callouts.p: Speed of EM waves in a vacuum = 3 x 10^8 m/s. Learn it: some questions expect you to know it.
Same speed does NOT mean same frequency or wavelength. Different parts of the spectrum have very different wavelengths and frequencies.

core.p: The wave equation from Topic 4 applies to all EM waves: **wave speed = frequency x wavelength**, v = f x wavelength. Since v is fixed at 3 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum, frequency and wavelength are **inversely proportional**.
bullets: v = f x wavelength, with v in m/s, f in hertz (Hz), wavelength in metres (m).
Rearranged: f = v / wavelength and wavelength = v / f.
If frequency doubles, wavelength halves (speed stays constant).
Long wavelength waves (radio) have low frequency; short wavelength waves (gamma) have high frequency.
Watch prefixes: kHz = 10^3 Hz, MHz = 10^6 Hz, GHz = 10^9 Hz; nm = 10^-9 m.

fig.cap: Radio waves and X-rays travel at the same speed c in a vacuum. Because v = f x wavelength and v is fixed, the short-wavelength X-ray must have a much higher frequency.

core.h: Transferring energy from source to observer
core.p: Every EM wave carries energy away from the thing that emits it (the **source**) to the thing that absorbs it (the **observer** or **absorber**). When the wave is absorbed, the energy is transferred to the absorber, often heating it or causing a chemical or electrical change.
bullets: The source emits the radiation, energy travels as the wave, the absorber gains the energy.
Energy is transferred **without any matter moving** from source to observer.
EM waves can transfer energy across a vacuum: no medium is needed.
The observer does not have to be a person: it can be a detector, an aerial, a solar cell, the skin, or a photographic film.
Higher-frequency EM waves carry more energy (this links to their hazards in 5.20-5.21).

callouts.p: The source is the object that emits the EM radiation; the observer (absorber) is the object that receives and absorbs it, gaining energy.

core.h: Examples of energy transfer by EM waves
core.p: Exam questions on 5.8 ask for examples. Each good example names the **source**, the **type of EM wave** and the **effect on the observer/absorber** that shows energy has been transferred.
bullets: **Sun to Earth**: visible light and infrared from the Sun warm the Earth's surface and drive photosynthesis.
**Microwave oven**: microwaves from the magnetron are absorbed by water molecules in food, which heats up.
**Grill or toaster**: infrared from the hot element is absorbed by the bread, raising its temperature.
**Radio transmitter to aerial**: radio waves cause tiny alternating currents in a receiving aerial (energy to electrical signal).
**Sunbathing**: ultraviolet from the Sun is absorbed by skin, causing tanning or sunburn.
**Solar cells**: light absorbed by a solar panel is transferred to electrical energy.
**X-ray imaging**: X-rays from the tube are absorbed by the detector or film, changing it (and can ionise cells).
**Seeing**: light from a lamp is absorbed by cells in the retina, causing electrical signals to the brain.

core.h: Why the energy transfer is useful and harmful
core.p: The same idea, that EM waves carry energy to whatever absorbs them, explains both their uses and their dangers.
bullets: Useful: heating (infrared, microwaves), communications (radio, microwaves), photosynthesis and vision (visible).
Harmful: absorbed ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays carry enough energy to **ionise** atoms and damage cells.
The amount of energy depends on the type of radiation (frequency) and on how much is absorbed.
Energy is only transferred to an object if the wave is **absorbed** by it; if it is transmitted or reflected, the object does not gain that energy.

callouts.t: Use the words source and observer
callouts.p: Mark schemes for 5.8 often reward stating that energy is transferred from the source to the observer/absorber, plus a named example.

core.p: Comparing EM waves with sound and water waves is a common way to test 5.7.
bullets: EM waves: transverse, can travel through a vacuum, all at 3 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum.
Sound: longitudinal, needs a medium, about 330 m/s in air (much slower).
Water waves: transverse, need water, travel slowly (a few m/s).
Lightning: the flash (light) arrives almost instantly, the thunder (sound) arrives later because light is about a million times faster.

core.p: Because the speed is constant, you can use **distance = speed x time** (x = v x t) to find how far EM waves travel or how long they take.
bullets: Distance = speed x time; time = distance / speed.
Convert km to m (x 1000) before using 3 x 10^8 m/s.
Radar and satellite signals: remember a reflected signal travels there and back (double the distance).
Use standard form carefully on your calculator: 3 x 10^8 is entered as 3 EXP 8.

callouts.p: For a radar or reflection question, the time measured is for the round trip; halve it (or double the distance) as appropriate.

core.p: Grade 9 answers link the facts together rather than listing them.
bullets: Because v is the same for all EM waves in a vacuum, they can only differ in frequency and wavelength: this is what defines their position in the spectrum.
Since they need no medium, EM waves are the only way energy reaches Earth from the Sun.
Energy transferred depends on absorption: the same infrared that warms a black surface is largely reflected by a shiny one.
Higher frequency means more energy carried per photon, which is why gamma is more dangerous than radio at the same intensity (link to 5.20).

analogy.t: A stadium Mexican wave across a crowd
analogy.p: In a Mexican wave each fan stands up and sits down (oscillating up and down) while the wave itself travels sideways round the stadium, just as in a transverse EM wave the oscillations are at right angles to the direction of energy transfer. Nobody moves round the stadium, yet the 'disturbance' gets from one side to the other, just as energy, not matter, travels from source to observer. Where it breaks down: a Mexican wave needs people (a medium), but EM waves need no medium at all and can cross a vacuum; also every EM wave goes at exactly the same speed in a vacuum, whereas crowd waves go at whatever speed people react.

terms.d: A transverse wave of oscillating electric and magnetic fields that transfers energy and can travel through a vacuum.
A wave in which the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
A wave in which the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer, e.g. sound.
A space containing no particles (no matter), such as outer space.
The speed of all EM waves in a vacuum: 3 x 10^8 m/s.
The material (solid, liquid or gas) a wave travels through; EM waves do not need one.
The object that emits the EM radiation.
The object that receives and absorbs the EM radiation, gaining energy.
The distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave, e.g. peak to peak, in metres.
The number of waves passing a point each second, in hertz (Hz).
The maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed (rest) position.
The distance travelled by a wave each second, in m/s; v = f x wavelength.
The unit of frequency: one wave per second.
The movement of energy from one place or store to another; EM waves transfer energy without transferring matter.

mistakes.r: All EM waves are transverse: oscillations perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.

mistakes.w: Transverse means the wave moves up and down.
mistakes.r: The oscillations are at right angles to the direction of energy transfer; the wave travels forwards.

mistakes.w: Gamma rays travel faster than radio waves because they have more energy.
mistakes.r: All EM waves travel at the same speed (3 x 10^8 m/s) in a vacuum; they differ in frequency and wavelength.

mistakes.w: EM waves travel at the speed of sound / need air to travel.
mistakes.r: EM waves need no medium and travel through a vacuum at 3 x 10^8 m/s; sound needs a medium.

mistakes.w: EM waves transfer particles / matter from the source.
mistakes.r: EM waves transfer energy, not matter, from source to observer.

mistakes.w: Only light and infrared transfer energy.
mistakes.r: All EM waves transfer energy from source to observer, e.g. radio waves induce currents in an aerial.

mistakes.w: Same speed means same frequency.
mistakes.r: Same speed means frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional; each part of the spectrum has a different frequency.

mistakes.w: Example: 'the sun gives off heat'.
mistakes.r: Name the wave, source and absorber: infrared from the Sun is absorbed by the Earth's surface, which warms up.

mistakes.w: Speed of EM waves is 3 x 10^6 m/s or 300 m/s.

exam.q: State the type of wave that all electromagnetic waves are.
model: Transverse.
exam.tip: One word answer; do not write 'longitudinal' or 'mechanical'.

exam.q: State the speed of electromagnetic waves in a vacuum. Give the unit.
exam.tip: The unit must be included for the mark.

exam.q: Describe the difference between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave.
model: In a transverse wave the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
In a longitudinal wave the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
exam.tip: Use 'direction of energy transfer' or 'direction of wave travel', not just 'the wave'.

exam.q: Which of these is the same for both microwaves and X-rays in a vacuum? A frequency B wavelength C speed D energy
model: C speed.
exam.tip: Only speed is shared by all EM waves in a vacuum.

exam.q: Explain why we can see light from the Sun but cannot hear sound from it.
model: Light is an EM wave, which can travel through a vacuum / does not need a medium.
Sound needs a medium (particles) to travel, and space is a vacuum.
exam.tip: Two linked points: one about light, one about sound.

exam.q: Give two examples of electromagnetic waves transferring energy from a source to an observer.
model: e.g. infrared from the Sun (source) warms the Earth / skin (observer).
e.g. microwaves from an oven heat water in food; radio waves induce a current in an aerial; light absorbed by a solar cell.
exam.tip: Each example needs the wave and what absorbs the energy.

exam.q: A radio station broadcasts at 100 MHz. Calculate the wavelength. Speed of EM waves = 3 x 10^8 m/s.
model: Convert: 100 MHz = 1.0 x 10^8 Hz.
wavelength = v / f = 3 x 10^8 / 1.0 x 10^8.
exam.tip: Convert MHz to Hz first; mega = 10^6.

exam.q: Explain how a microwave oven shows that electromagnetic waves transfer energy from a source to an observer.
model: Microwaves are emitted by the oven (the source).
The microwaves are absorbed by water molecules in the food (the observer/absorber).
Energy is transferred to the thermal store of the food, so its temperature rises.
exam.tip: Follow the energy: emitted, travels, absorbed, effect.

exam.q: Light from the Sun takes 500 s to reach the Earth. Calculate the distance from the Sun to the Earth.
model: distance = speed x time = 3 x 10^8 x 500.
exam.tip: Give your answer in standard form with the unit.

exam.q: Explain, using properties of electromagnetic waves, why gamma rays and visible light from a distant supernova arrive at the Earth at the same time, and why gamma rays have a much shorter wavelength.
model: All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum (3 x 10^8 m/s).
So they cover the same distance through space in the same time.
v = f x wavelength and v is constant.
Gamma rays have a much higher frequency, so their wavelength must be much shorter.
exam.tip: Link the constant speed to the wave equation for the last two marks.

exam.q: Describe the properties of electromagnetic waves and explain, with examples, how they transfer energy.
model: All EM waves are transverse.
Oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
They all travel at the same speed, 3 x 10^8 m/s, in a vacuum and need no medium.
They transfer energy, not matter, from a source to an observer/absorber.
Example: infrared/light from the Sun is absorbed by the Earth and warms it; travels through the vacuum of space.
Example: microwaves heat food / radio waves induce a current in an aerial / UV causes sunburn.
exam.tip: A 6 mark answer needs properties AND at least two well-explained examples, written as linked sentences.

worked.q: A Wi-Fi router emits microwaves with a frequency of 2.4 GHz. Calculate their wavelength in a vacuum.
steps: Write the equation: wavelength = v / f.
Convert the frequency: 2.4 GHz = 2.4 x 10^9 Hz.
Substitute: wavelength = 3 x 10^8 / 2.4 x 10^9.
Calculate: wavelength = 0.125 m.

worked.q: A radar pulse is sent to an aircraft and the reflected pulse returns after 0.0002 s. How far away is the aircraft?
steps: Total distance travelled = speed x time = 3 x 10^8 x 0.0002 = 60 000 m.
The pulse went there and back, so halve it: 60 000 / 2 = 30 000 m.
Convert: 30 000 m = 30 km.

worked.q: Model answer: explain, with an example, that electromagnetic waves transfer energy from source to observer.
steps: State the idea: all EM waves transfer energy from the source that emits them to the observer that absorbs them, without transferring matter.
Name the source and wave: the Sun emits infrared radiation and visible light.
Describe the path: the waves travel through the vacuum of space at 3 x 10^8 m/s; no medium is needed.
Describe the absorber and effect: the Earth's surface absorbs the radiation, so energy is transferred to its thermal store and it warms up.
worked.ans: Infrared and light from the Sun (source) cross the vacuum of space and are absorbed by the Earth (observer), raising its temperature.

phy_edx.4.4.summary: In this core practical you shine a narrow ray of light from a ray box into a rectangular glass block at different angles of incidence, trace the rays on paper, and measure the angles of incidence and refraction from the **normal** with a protractor. Light **slows down** when it enters glass, so it bends **towards the normal**; when it leaves the block it speeds up and bends **away from the normal**, emerging parallel to the incident ray. The results show the angle of refraction is always smaller than the angle of incidence (except at 0 degrees, when there is no change in direction), and you explain this using the change in wave speed as EM waves interact with the matter in the glass.

core.p: Edexcel core practical 5.9: **investigate refraction in rectangular glass blocks in terms of the interaction of electromagnetic waves with matter**. You need to be able to describe the method, take and process the readings, and explain the results using changes in speed.
bullets: Independent variable: **angle of incidence** (i).
Dependent variable: **angle of refraction** (r) (and you can also observe the emergent ray).
Control variables: same glass block (same material), same ray box and slit, same wavelength/colour of light, same face of block.
Can be extended by comparing blocks of different materials (e.g. glass and Perspex) at the same angle of incidence.
Questions can ask for method, risks, sources of error, analysis of a table or graph, and explanation of results.

callouts.p: Refraction happens because light changes speed when it crosses a boundary between materials of different density. Slower in glass means bending towards the normal.

core.p: Each item has a reason, and exam questions often ask why a piece of equipment is used.
bullets: **Ray box** with a power supply: a bright light source.
**Single slit**: produces a **narrow ray** so the centre of the ray can be marked accurately.
**Rectangular glass block** (or Perspex): the material being tested.
**Plain white paper** (A3 or A4): to draw the outline and trace the rays on.
**Sharp pencil and ruler**: thin, accurate lines.
**Protractor**: to measure angles to the nearest degree.
Optional: coloured filter to give one colour, so the ray does not spread into a spectrum.

core.p: This is the sequence examiners reward in a 6 mark method question.
bullets: 1. Place the glass block on a sheet of plain paper and **draw round its outline** with a sharp pencil.
2. Remove the block and draw a **normal** (a line at 90 degrees to the surface) at a point on one long side, using a protractor.
3. Use the protractor to draw lines at angles of incidence from the normal, e.g. 10, 20, 30 ... 70 degrees.
4. Replace the block exactly on its outline.
5. Shine a narrow ray from the ray box along one of the incidence lines so it hits the block where the normal meets the surface.
6. Mark the **emergent ray** with two crosses (far apart) where it leaves the opposite side of the block.
7. Remove the block, join the crosses to the opposite face and draw the line where the ray left; join the entry point to the exit point to show the **refracted ray** inside the block.
8. Measure the **angle of refraction** between the refracted ray and the normal.
9. Repeat for each angle of incidence; repeat the whole experiment and calculate a mean for each angle.

callouts.p: Both angles are measured between the ray and the normal, never between the ray and the surface of the block.

core.p: Your traced diagram should show an incident ray, the normal, the refracted ray inside the block and the emergent ray. The emergent ray is **parallel** to the incident ray but shifted sideways.
bullets: Entering the glass (air to glass): ray bends **towards the normal**, so r is less than i.
Leaving the glass (glass to air): ray bends **away from the normal**.
Because the two faces are parallel, the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray (a sideways or lateral shift).
At i = 0 degrees (along the normal) the ray passes straight through without changing direction, though it still slows down.
Some light is also reflected at each surface: you may see a faint reflected ray.

callouts.p: A construction line drawn at 90 degrees (perpendicular) to the surface at the point where the ray hits it.
The change in direction of a wave as it passes from one medium into another, caused by a change in its speed.

core.h: Explaining the results: change in speed
core.p: This is the key physics. Light is an EM wave; when it enters glass, it interacts with the particles of the glass and **slows down**. The change in speed causes the change in direction.
bullets: Light travels at about 3 x 10^8 m/s in air and roughly 2 x 10^8 m/s in glass.
Going from air into glass (a more **optically dense** material): speed decreases, ray bends **towards** the normal.
Going from glass into air (less dense): speed increases, ray bends **away from** the normal.
The **frequency stays the same**; because v = f x wavelength, the **wavelength decreases** in glass.
Along the normal (i = 0) the whole wavefront slows at the same moment, so the direction does not change.

callouts.p: Slows down: bends towards the normal. Speeds up: bends away from the normal.

core.p: A grade 9 answer explains why a change in speed causes a change in direction, using wavefronts.
bullets: A wavefront is a line joining the same point (e.g. crest) on neighbouring waves.
When a ray hits the block at an angle, one end of each wavefront enters the glass first and slows down first.
The other end is still in air travelling faster, so it catches up: the wavefront **swivels** round.
This changes the direction of travel towards the normal.
Inside the glass the wavefronts are **closer together** (shorter wavelength) because the wave is slower but the frequency is unchanged.

core.h: Interaction of EM waves with matter
core.p: The spec wording asks you to link refraction to how EM waves interact with matter. Different materials affect light differently.
bullets: Light passing through a transparent material is **transmitted** but slowed by interaction with the atoms in the material.
Some light is **reflected** at each boundary and a little may be **absorbed** in the block.
Different materials slow light by different amounts, so they refract it by different amounts (e.g. glass refracts more than water, Perspex similar to glass).
Different colours (wavelengths) slow by slightly different amounts in glass, so white light can spread out (dispersion) a little; using one colour or a filter keeps the ray sharp.

core.p: Questions often ask for one hazard and how to reduce the risk.
bullets: **Ray box gets hot**: do not touch the bulb/housing; let it cool before moving it.
**Darkened room**: trip hazard; keep bags and stools under desks, move carefully.
**Glass block can chip or break**: handle with care; report chipped blocks (sharp edges).
**Bright light**: do not look directly into the ray box beam.
Electrical supply: keep water away from the power pack.

head: Hazard
Risk
Control measure
rows: Do not touch; allow to cool

core.p: Knowing why results may be inaccurate, and how to improve, is regularly examined.
bullets: **Wide ray**: hard to find its centre; use a narrow single slit and mark the centre of the ray.
**Thick pencil lines**: use a sharp pencil to reduce uncertainty in angle measurement.
**Crosses too close together**: mark them far apart so the direction of the emergent ray is accurate.
**Block moved**: keep it on its outline; any shift changes the entry/exit points.
**Protractor reading**: read at eye level and place the centre exactly on the point where the ray meets the normal.
**Random error**: repeat each angle and calculate a mean.
Taking measurements in a darkened room makes the ray easier to see.

callouts.p: Measuring from the surface gives 90 degrees minus the correct angle. Always measure from the normal.

core.p: Higher-mark questions may ask you to describe a pattern, compare materials, or evaluate a conclusion.
bullets: Describe a trend using the data: 'as the angle of incidence increases from 10 to 70 degrees, the angle of refraction increases from 7 to 38 degrees'.
State that r is always smaller than i, so light bends towards the normal on entering glass.
Comparing materials: the material with the smaller angle of refraction at the same i slows light more (it is more optically dense).
Precise data: repeat readings close together. Accurate data: close to the true value.
A conclusion should link the pattern to a cause: light slows down in glass.

analogy.t: A marching band walking from a road onto mud
analogy.p: Imagine a row of marchers (a wavefront) walking diagonally from smooth tarmac onto thick mud. The marchers at one end reach the mud first and slow down, while the others are still on tarmac moving fast, so the whole row swings round and changes direction towards the normal. Walking back onto tarmac, the first to leave speeds up and the row swings the other way. If they walk straight onto the mud (along the normal), everyone slows together and the direction does not change. Where it breaks down: marchers can choose their speed and step size, but light's frequency is fixed by the source and its speed is set by the material; also light does not lose energy just by slowing in the way tired marchers would.

terms.d: The change in direction of a wave when it passes from one medium to another, caused by a change in speed.
A line at 90 degrees to a surface at the point where the ray meets it; angles are measured from it.
The angle between the incident ray and the normal.
The angle between the refracted ray and the normal.
The ray travelling towards the boundary before it is refracted.
The ray after it has changed direction at a boundary, here inside the glass.
The ray leaving the block; parallel to the incident ray for a rectangular block.
Describes a material in which light travels more slowly; glass is more optically dense than air.
A line joining equivalent points (e.g. all the crests) on neighbouring waves.
A light source with a slit that produces a narrow beam (ray) of light.
The variable you change: here the angle of incidence.
The variable you measure: here the angle of refraction.
A variable kept the same so the test is fair, e.g. the material of the block.
Unpredictable variation in readings; reduced by repeating and taking a mean.
The sideways shift between the incident ray and the parallel emergent ray.

mistakes.w: Measure the angle between the ray and the edge of the block.
mistakes.r: Measure the angles between the ray and the normal.

mistakes.w: Light speeds up in glass so it bends.
mistakes.r: Light slows down in glass, so it bends towards the normal.

mistakes.w: Light bends away from the normal when it enters the glass.
mistakes.r: It bends towards the normal entering glass and away from the normal leaving glass.

mistakes.w: The frequency changes in the glass.
mistakes.r: Frequency stays the same; speed and wavelength decrease.

mistakes.w: Refraction happens because the light hits the block.
mistakes.r: Refraction is caused by the change in speed at the boundary between two materials.

mistakes.w: At 0 degrees the light bends the most.
mistakes.r: At 0 degrees (along the normal) there is no change in direction, though the speed still changes.

mistakes.w: Use a wide beam so it is easier to see.
mistakes.r: Use a narrow ray (single slit) so its centre can be marked accurately.

mistakes.w: The angle of refraction is directly proportional to the angle of incidence.
mistakes.r: r increases as i increases but the relationship is not directly proportional (the graph curves).

mistakes.w: Hazard: the light is dangerous / radiation.
mistakes.r: A sensible hazard: the ray box gets hot (burns), or tripping in a darkened room.

exam.q: State what is meant by the normal.
model: A line at 90 degrees (perpendicular) to the surface where the ray meets it.
exam.tip: Say 'at right angles to the surface'.

exam.q: Name the piece of equipment used to measure the angles of incidence and refraction.
model: Protractor.
exam.tip: Simple recall.

exam.q: State the independent and dependent variables in this investigation.
model: Independent: angle of incidence.
Dependent: angle of refraction.
exam.tip: Independent is what you change; dependent is what you measure.

exam.q: Give one hazard in this experiment and how to reduce the risk.
model: Ray box becomes hot / can cause burns.
Do not touch it / allow to cool before handling.
exam.tip: Match the control measure to the hazard you named.

exam.q: Explain why a ray of light changes direction when it enters a glass block at an angle.
model: Light slows down when it enters glass.
The change in speed causes it to change direction / bend towards the normal.
exam.tip: 'Speed' is the key word.

exam.q: A ray enters a glass block along the normal. Describe what happens to the ray.
model: It does not change direction / passes straight through.
Its speed decreases (and wavelength decreases).
exam.tip: No bending does not mean no change in speed.

exam.q: Suggest two ways a student could improve the accuracy of the angles measured.
model: Use a narrow ray / mark the centre of the ray.
Mark crosses far apart / use a sharp pencil / repeat and take a mean / do it in a darkened room.
exam.tip: Any two distinct, specific improvements.

exam.q: A student finds that at an angle of incidence of 40 degrees the angle of refraction is 25 degrees for glass and 30 degrees for water. Explain what this shows.
model: Both angles of refraction are less than 40 degrees, so light bends towards the normal in both.
Glass gives the smaller angle of refraction so it refracts light more.
So light slows down more in glass than in water.
exam.tip: Link the size of the bending to the change in speed.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of wavefronts, why light bends towards the normal when it passes from air into glass.
model: One side of the wavefront reaches the glass first and slows down first.
The rest of the wavefront is still in air and moving faster.
So the wavefront turns / changes direction towards the normal.
exam.tip: Describe the two ends of the wavefront travelling at different speeds.

exam.q: Describe how to carry out an investigation to measure how the angle of refraction depends on the angle of incidence for a rectangular glass block.
model: Place the block on paper and draw around it.
Draw a normal to one surface with a protractor.
Shine a narrow ray from a ray box (with a slit) at the block where the normal meets it.
Mark the path of the emergent ray with crosses; remove the block and join the points to draw the refracted ray.
Measure the angles of incidence and refraction from the normal with a protractor.
Repeat for a range of angles of incidence (e.g. 10 to 70 degrees) and repeat to calculate a mean.
exam.tip: Write the steps in a logical order; include what you measure, with what, and how you get a range and repeats.

exam.q: Describe and explain the path of a ray of light that enters one side of a rectangular glass block at an angle of 45 degrees and leaves through the opposite side.
model: On entering, the ray bends towards the normal (angle of refraction less than 45 degrees).
Because light slows down in glass.
On leaving, the ray bends away from the normal because it speeds up.
Emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray (displaced sideways).
exam.tip: Two direction changes, each with its speed reason.

worked.q: Use the table of results (i = 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70 degrees; r = 7, 13, 19, 25, 30, 35, 38 degrees) to describe the relationship and draw a conclusion.
steps: Look at the trend: as i increases, r increases.
Compare each pair: r is always less than i, so the ray bends towards the normal.
Check proportionality: doubling i from 30 to 60 degrees raises r from 19 to 35 degrees, not 38, so it is not directly proportional.
Explain: light slows down as it enters glass, so it bends towards the normal.
worked.ans: The angle of refraction increases with the angle of incidence but is always smaller, and they are not directly proportional; this is because light slows down when it enters the glass.

worked.q: Three repeat readings of the angle of refraction for i = 50 degrees are 30, 31 and 36 degrees. Find the mean.
steps: Identify the anomaly: 36 degrees is far from the other two readings.
Exclude it (or repeat that reading).
Mean = (30 + 31) / 2 = 30.5 degrees.
Round sensibly to the resolution of the protractor: about 31 degrees (or 30.5 degrees).
worked.ans: Mean = 30.5 degrees (anomaly of 36 degrees excluded)

worked.q: Light travels at 3.0 x 10^8 m/s in air and 2.0 x 10^8 m/s in glass. Red light has a frequency of 4.5 x 10^14 Hz. Find its wavelength in air and in glass.
steps: wavelength = v / f.
Frequency is unchanged in the glass.
worked.ans: Air: 6.7 x 10^-7 m; glass: 4.4 x 10^-7 m (shorter because the wave is slower)

phy_edx.4.5.summary: Electromagnetic waves form a **continuous spectrum**: there are no gaps, and the familiar groups (radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays) are just convenient ranges. In that order the groups have **decreasing wavelength and increasing frequency** (and the energy they carry increases), while all travel at the same speed in a vacuum. Our eyes can detect only a **very limited range** of these frequencies, visible light, which itself is a continuous spectrum grouped in order as **red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet**, with red having the longest wavelength and violet the highest frequency.

core.p: Spec points 5.10 to 5.12 are all recall, but they underpin almost every other EM question, and order errors cost marks every year.
bullets: 5.10: recall that EM waves form a **continuous spectrum** and are grouped in order of **decreasing wavelength and increasing frequency**: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.
5.11: recall that our **eyes can only detect a limited range of frequencies** of EM radiation.
5.12: recall the main groupings of the **continuous visible spectrum**, in order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
Links to 5.7-5.8 (all transverse, same speed in a vacuum) and to the wave equation v = f x wavelength.

callouts.p: Radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays: wavelength decreasing, frequency increasing.

core.p: Learn the seven groups in order. A mnemonic helps: **Rich Men In Vegas Use eXpensive Gadgets** (Radio, Microwaves, Infrared, Visible, Ultraviolet, X-rays, Gamma).
bullets: From radio to gamma: **wavelength decreases**, **frequency increases**.
From radio to gamma: the **energy** carried by the radiation increases (and so does the potential for harm, see 5.20).
Exam questions often give a partly filled spectrum and ask you to name the missing groups.
Be able to work in either direction: gamma to radio means wavelength increasing and frequency decreasing.

core.p: A continuous spectrum has **every possible wavelength** between the extremes with **no gaps**. The named groups are human labels; their edges blur into each other.
bullets: There is no sudden jump between, say, infrared and visible: wavelengths change smoothly.
Neighbouring groups **overlap**: e.g. some short microwaves have similar wavelengths to long infrared; X-rays and gamma rays overlap in wavelength.
X-rays and gamma rays are distinguished by **how they are produced** (gamma from changes in the nucleus; X-rays from electrons), not just wavelength (links to 5.24).
The visible spectrum is also continuous: red fades into orange into yellow and so on.

callouts.p: A spectrum containing all wavelengths (and frequencies) over a range, with no gaps between them.
Do not say EM waves are seven different kinds of wave. They are all the same kind of wave, differing only in wavelength and frequency.

core.p: All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum, 3 x 10^8 m/s. From v = f x wavelength, if v is fixed, **frequency is inversely proportional to wavelength**.
bullets: Shorter wavelength means higher frequency.
Doubling the frequency halves the wavelength.
f = v / wavelength; wavelength = v / f.
This is why you can describe the order using either quantity: 'decreasing wavelength' and 'increasing frequency' mean the same thing for EM waves.
Units: wavelength in metres (m), frequency in hertz (Hz).

fig.cap: Radio waves, visible light and gamma rays drawn to compare wavelength. All travel at the same speed, so the one with the shortest wavelength (gamma) has the highest frequency.

core.p: You do not need exact values, but knowing rough orders of magnitude helps with calculation questions and with putting groups in order.
bullets: Radio waves have the longest wavelengths, from about 10 cm up to many kilometres.
Visible light is roughly 400 nm to 700 nm (4 x 10^-7 m to 7 x 10^-7 m).
Gamma rays have the shortest wavelengths, around 10^-12 m or less.
Approximate values below are for guidance; boundaries are not sharp.

callouts.p: Each step along the spectrum is roughly a factor of 100 to 1000 in wavelength. Use this to sanity-check answers.

core.h: Our eyes detect only a limited range
core.p: The human eye responds only to a **narrow band** of frequencies, which we call **visible light**. All the other groups are invisible to us, even though they are the same kind of wave.
bullets: Visible light is a tiny fraction of the whole EM spectrum.
Cells in the retina (rods and cones) absorb visible light and send signals to the brain; they do not respond to infrared, ultraviolet etc.
We need **detectors** for other groups: aerials for radio, thermal imaging cameras for infrared, photographic film or digital detectors for X-rays, Geiger-Muller tubes for gamma.
Some animals detect slightly different ranges, e.g. bees see some ultraviolet, some snakes sense infrared.

callouts.p: Our eyes can only detect a limited range of frequencies of electromagnetic radiation.

core.p: Visible light is itself a **continuous spectrum** of colours. It is grouped, in order of decreasing wavelength and increasing frequency, as **red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet** (ROYGBIV, 'Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain').
bullets: **Red**: longest wavelength (about 700 nm), lowest frequency, lowest energy of visible light.
**Violet**: shortest wavelength (about 400 nm), highest frequency, highest energy of visible light.
Red is next to infrared ('below red'); violet is next to ultraviolet ('beyond violet').
White light is a mixture of all the colours of the visible spectrum.
The colours blend smoothly: there are no sharp lines between them.

core.p: A **prism** separates white light into its colours (**dispersion**). This shows that white light contains the whole visible spectrum.
bullets: Different colours slow down by slightly different amounts in glass, so they refract by different amounts.
Violet is refracted (bent) the most, red the least.
The result is a continuous band of colour, the same order as a rainbow.
Raindrops act like tiny prisms to produce a rainbow.

core.p: Moving along the spectrum from radio to gamma, the **energy** carried by the radiation increases with frequency. This explains why the high-frequency end is more hazardous.
bullets: Radio, microwaves, infrared and visible: lower frequency, non-ionising.
Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma: higher frequency, carry enough energy to ionise atoms (detail in 5.20-5.21).
So 'increasing frequency' also means 'increasing energy' and 'increasing danger' when absorbed.

callouts.p: Higher frequency does not mean faster. Every group travels at 3 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum.

core.p: Use v = f x wavelength with v = 3 x 10^8 m/s to convert between frequency and wavelength, then use the answer to identify the group.
bullets: Write the equation, substitute with units in standard form, then calculate.
Prefixes: kHz 10^3, MHz 10^6, GHz 10^9 Hz; mm 10^-3, micrometre 10^-6, nm 10^-9 m.
Check your answer against typical ranges: a frequency of 5 x 10^14 Hz should give a visible wavelength (about 600 nm).
Give answers in standard form to 2 or 3 significant figures.

core.p: Order questions are quick marks if you are precise.
bullets: Always state the direction: 'from radio waves to gamma rays, wavelength decreases'.
When comparing two groups, say which has the longer wavelength AND which has the higher frequency if asked.
Spell groups correctly and use full names: 'ultraviolet', 'X-rays', 'gamma rays'.
If asked for a property shared by all groups: transverse, same speed in a vacuum, transfer energy, can travel through a vacuum.

analogy.t: A piano keyboard that never ends
analogy.p: Think of the EM spectrum as a huge piano keyboard stretching for kilometres. Low notes on the left are radio waves (long wavelength, low frequency); high notes on the right are gamma rays (short wavelength, high frequency). Our eyes are like a listener who can only hear about one octave in the middle (visible light), and within that octave the notes run from red (lowest) to violet (highest). Where it breaks down: a piano has separate keys with gaps between notes, but the EM spectrum is continuous with every frequency in between; and unlike sound, all EM waves travel at the same speed and need no medium.

phy_edx.4.6.summary: Different substances can **absorb**, **transmit**, **refract** or **reflect** electromagnetic waves, and what happens depends on both the substance and the **wavelength** of the wave: glass transmits visible light but absorbs much ultraviolet, and bone absorbs X-rays that pass through soft tissue. At Higher tier you must explain that **refraction** happens because EM waves travel at **different speeds** in different substances: when wavefronts meet a boundary at an angle, one end slows down first so the wave changes direction. The **frequency stays the same**, so a slower wave has a **shorter wavelength** (v = f x λ).

core.h: What can happen when an EM wave meets a substance
core.p: When an electromagnetic wave reaches a new substance, its energy can be **absorbed**, **transmitted**, **refracted** or **reflected** (and usually a mixture of these happens at once). The spec says these effects **vary with wavelength**: the same substance can treat one part of the spectrum completely differently from another.
bullets: **Absorbed**: the wave's energy is taken in by the substance and the wave stops; the energy usually increases the substance's **thermal energy store** (it warms up).
**Transmitted**: the wave passes **through** the substance and carries on out the other side.
**Refracted**: the wave **changes direction** as it crosses a boundary between two substances at an angle, because its **speed changes**.
**Reflected**: the wave **bounces back** off the surface into the substance it came from.
A transmitted wave is often refracted too, and part of almost every wave is reflected at a boundary.
Energy is conserved: energy reflected + energy absorbed + energy transmitted = energy of the incident wave.

core.h: Why the effect depends on wavelength
core.p: Whether a wave is absorbed, transmitted or reflected depends on how it interacts with the **particles (atoms, molecules and electrons)** of the substance, and that interaction depends on the wave's **wavelength (and so its frequency)**. A substance that is transparent to one wavelength can be opaque to another.
bullets: **Glass** transmits visible light but **absorbs much of the ultraviolet** that hits it, which is why you do not get sunburnt through a closed window as easily.
**Skin and flesh** absorb visible light and ultraviolet, but **X-rays** are mostly transmitted through soft tissue.
**Bone** is denser and absorbs X-rays far more than soft tissue does, so bones show up as pale shadows on an X-ray image.
**Water** absorbs microwaves and infrared strongly, so food containing water heats up in a microwave oven.
**Metals** reflect radio waves and microwaves, and most metals reflect visible light well when polished.
So you must always say **which wavelength** you are talking about: 'glass is transparent' is only true for visible light.

callouts.p: Different substances may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect electromagnetic waves in ways that vary with wavelength.

core.p: Exam questions often give you a substance and a type of EM wave and ask what happens, or ask you to explain a use. Learn these pairings and the reason behind each.
bullets: Radio waves pass through walls and buildings fairly easily, so you can listen to a radio indoors.
Microwaves pass through glass and most plastics (the container stays cooler) but are absorbed by water molecules in food.
The metal mesh in a microwave oven door **reflects** the microwaves back in, but has holes small enough to let **visible light** (much shorter wavelength) through so you can see the food.
Infrared is absorbed by most surfaces, especially dull black ones, warming them.
Lead and thick concrete **absorb** X-rays and gamma rays, which is why they are used as shielding.
Gamma rays are very penetrating: they are transmitted through most materials and only significantly absorbed by thick, dense materials.

callouts.p: A favourite 2-mark explanation: the mesh reflects microwaves (long wavelength) but transmits visible light (short wavelength). The effect depends on wavelength.

core.h: The atmosphere as a wavelength filter
core.p: The Earth's atmosphere is a good example of one substance behaving differently for different wavelengths. Some parts of the spectrum reach the ground; others are absorbed high up.
bullets: **Visible light** and many **radio waves** are transmitted through the atmosphere, so we can see the Sun and use ground-based radio telescopes.
The **ozone layer** absorbs much of the Sun's **ultraviolet**, protecting living things from the most harmful UV.
Gases such as **water vapour and carbon dioxide** absorb some **infrared**.
**X-rays and gamma rays** from space are absorbed by the atmosphere, which is why X-ray telescopes have to be put on satellites above it.
Some radio waves are **reflected** by a charged layer high in the atmosphere (the ionosphere), letting them travel around the curve of the Earth.

callouts.p: Absorption of EM waves transfers energy to the absorbing substance, so the atmosphere is warmed by the infrared it absorbs.

core.p: These words describe how a material treats **visible light**, but the same idea applies to any wavelength: a material can be 'transparent to radio waves' or 'opaque to ultraviolet'.
bullets: **Transparent**: transmits the waves without scattering them, so you can see clearly through it (clear glass for visible light).
**Translucent**: transmits the waves but scatters them, so images are blurred (frosted glass).
**Opaque**: does not transmit the waves; they are absorbed or reflected (wood, metal for visible light).
Your body is opaque to visible light but largely transparent to X-rays and radio waves.
Always name the wavelength when you say a material is transparent or opaque.

core.p: EM waves **transfer energy**. When a wave is absorbed, that energy is transferred to the substance. What the energy then does depends on the wavelength.
bullets: Infrared and microwaves absorbed by a substance increase the **kinetic energy of its particles**, so its temperature rises.
Visible light absorbed by a dark surface heats it; absorbed by the retina it triggers vision.
Higher-frequency radiation (UV, X-rays, gamma) carries more energy per wave packet and, when absorbed, can **ionise** atoms and damage cells (covered in more detail under hazards).
Radio waves absorbed by a metal aerial can make electrons oscillate, producing an alternating current in a circuit.
More absorption means less transmission: a thicker or denser absorber lets less radiation through.

core.p: Reflection happens at the boundary between two substances. Smooth, shiny surfaces reflect well; how well a surface reflects depends on the wavelength as well as the surface.
bullets: Polished metal reflects visible light and infrared well, which is why survival blankets are shiny.
Metal dishes are used to reflect and focus microwaves and radio waves for satellite TV and radio telescopes.
White surfaces reflect most visible light; black surfaces absorb most visible light.
The **angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection**, both measured from the **normal**.
Even clear glass reflects a small fraction of the light hitting it, which is why you can see a faint reflection in a window.

core.h: Refraction: change of direction at a boundary
core.p: **Refraction** is the change in direction of a wave as it passes from one substance into another. It happens because the wave's **speed changes** at the boundary. This is the Higher-tier idea in 5.14: refraction is **due to differences in the velocity** of EM waves in different substances.
bullets: Light travels fastest in a vacuum and slightly slower in air; it is noticeably slower in water and slower still in glass.
If the wave enters the new substance **at an angle to the normal**, the speed change makes it **change direction**.
If the wave travels **along the normal** (at 90 degrees to the boundary) its **speed and wavelength still change** but it does **not change direction**.
Slowing down (e.g. air into glass) bends the wave **towards the normal**.
Speeding up (e.g. glass into air) bends the wave **away from the normal**.
The **normal** is an imaginary line drawn at 90 degrees to the boundary at the point where the wave hits it.

callouts.p: The change in direction of a wave when it passes from one medium into another, caused by a change in its speed.
Refraction is really a change in speed. Along the normal the speed still changes but the direction does not.

core.h: Speed of light in different substances (Higher)
core.p: All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum, about **3 x 10^8 m/s**. In a material they are slowed down by their interaction with the particles. The more the material slows the wave, the more the wave refracts when it enters at an angle.
bullets: Use **wave speed = frequency x wavelength**, v = f x λ, with v in m/s, f in Hz and λ in m.
Light is slowed most in glass in the examples below, so light bends more entering glass from air than entering water from air.
Air slows light only very slightly, so for calculations you can treat air as having the vacuum speed.
The values in the table are approximate; exam questions will always give you the speed you need.

callouts.t: Same speed only in a vacuum
callouts.p: EM waves all travel at 3 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum. In a substance they are slower, and the speed can be slightly different for different wavelengths.

core.p: A **wavefront** is a line joining points on a wave that are in step, such as all the crests. Wavefronts are drawn at right angles to the direction the wave travels. Drawing them is the clearest way to explain why a change in speed causes a change in direction.
bullets: The wavefronts approach the boundary **at an angle**, so **one end of each wavefront reaches the glass first**.
That end **slows down** while the rest of the wavefront, still in the air, carries on at the faster speed.
For a short time the two ends travel at **different speeds**, so the wavefront **pivots (swings round)**.
Once the whole wavefront is in the glass it travels in a **new direction, closer to the normal**.
The wavefronts are **closer together** in the glass: the wavelength is shorter because the wave is slower.
Leaving the glass the opposite happens: one end speeds up first and the wave bends away from the normal.

callouts.p: In a sketch, show wavefronts closer together in the slower medium, continuous at the boundary, and the new direction at right angles to the new wavefronts.
