core.h: Frequency stays the same, wavelength changes
core.p: When a wave crosses a boundary its **frequency does not change**: the number of waves arriving at the boundary each second must equal the number leaving it each second, or waves would pile up or vanish. Since v = f x λ and f is fixed, **wavelength is proportional to speed**.
bullets: Slower medium (glass, water): **same frequency, shorter wavelength**.
Faster medium (back into air): same frequency, longer wavelength.
The frequency is set by the **source**, not by the medium.
The colour of visible light depends on its frequency, so light does not change colour when it enters water or glass.
Ratio trick: λ in glass / λ in air = speed in glass / speed in air.

callouts.p: Never write that the frequency changes when light refracts. Speed and wavelength change; frequency stays the same.

fig.cap: The same wave passing through a glass block. The frequency stays the same, but because the wave is slower in glass its wavelength is shorter. When it leaves the glass it speeds up again and its wavelength returns to the original value.

core.h: Different wavelengths refract by different amounts
core.p: In glass, different wavelengths of light travel at very slightly different speeds. Violet light is slowed a little more than red light, so violet is refracted more. This is why a **prism** splits white light into a **spectrum**: the effect of refraction **varies with wavelength**, exactly as 5.13 says.
bullets: White light is a mixture of all the colours (wavelengths) of the visible spectrum.
On entering a prism each colour bends by a slightly different amount, so the colours spread out.
Red (longest visible wavelength) is refracted least; violet (shortest) is refracted most.
The flat sides of a rectangular glass block mean the colours come out parallel again and overlap, so you do not usually see the spread with a block.
This splitting of white light is called **dispersion**.

core.h: Pulling it together for the exam
core.p: Most marks on this point come from linking **what happens** (absorbed, transmitted, refracted, reflected) to **wavelength**, and, at Higher tier, linking **refraction** to a **change in speed** using wavefronts.
bullets: Name the effect using the correct verb and say which wavelength or part of the spectrum.
For refraction always mention **speed change**, then **direction change**, then **towards or away from the normal**.
For wavefront explanations mention that **one side of the wavefront slows first**.
In calculations, keep f the same and use v = f x λ in each medium.
Check powers of ten: visible light wavelengths are around 4 x 10^-7 m to 7 x 10^-7 m.

analogy.p: Picture a line of marchers (a wavefront) walking at an angle from a smooth road onto a muddy field. The marchers at one end reach the mud first and slow down, while the others are still on the road moving quickly. The line swings round and carries on in a new direction, closer to straight across the boundary (towards the normal). In the mud the rows are closer together (shorter wavelength) but the drummer still sets the same number of steps per second (same frequency). Where it breaks down: marchers are objects that can choose to stop, whereas a light wave is a transfer of energy, and light can also be partly reflected or absorbed at the boundary, which the marchers never are.

terms.d: When a substance takes in the energy of a wave so the wave does not continue; the energy is usually transferred to the substance's thermal energy store.
When a wave passes through a substance and continues out of the other side.
When a wave bounces back off a boundary into the medium it came from; angle of incidence = angle of reflection.
The change in direction of a wave as it passes from one medium into another, caused by a change in its speed.
The substance a wave is travelling through, such as air, water or glass (plural: media).
The surface where two different media meet.
An imaginary line drawn at 90 degrees to a boundary at the point where a ray meets it; angles are measured from it.
The angle between the incoming ray and the normal.
The angle between the refracted ray and the normal.
A line joining points on a wave that are in step (for example all the crests); drawn at right angles to the direction of travel.
The distance a wave travels per second, in m/s; v = f x λ.
The number of waves passing a point each second, in hertz (Hz); unchanged when a wave changes medium.
The distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave, such as crest to crest, in metres.
Transmits a given wavelength without scattering it, so objects can be seen clearly through it.
Does not transmit a given wavelength; the waves are absorbed or reflected.
The splitting of white light into its colours because different wavelengths are refracted by different amounts.

mistakes.r: Light refracts because its **speed changes** as it enters the glass; one side of the wavefront slows down first.

mistakes.w: The frequency changes when light goes into glass.
mistakes.r: Frequency stays the same; **speed and wavelength** decrease.

mistakes.w: Light speeds up in glass because glass is denser.
mistakes.r: Light **slows down** in glass (about 2 x 10^8 m/s compared with 3 x 10^8 m/s in air).

mistakes.w: Light always bends when it crosses a boundary.
mistakes.r: Along the normal the speed changes but the **direction does not change**.

mistakes.w: Entering glass, light bends away from the normal.
mistakes.r: Slowing down bends the ray **towards the normal**; speeding up (leaving the glass) bends it away.

mistakes.w: Angles are measured from the surface of the block.
mistakes.r: Angles of incidence and refraction are measured from the **normal**.

mistakes.w: Glass is transparent, so it lets all EM waves through.
mistakes.r: Glass transmits visible light but **absorbs much ultraviolet**: the effect depends on wavelength.

mistakes.w: X-rays bounce off bones, which is why bones show up.
mistakes.r: Bones **absorb** X-rays more than soft tissue, which **transmits** them; the detector behind is not exposed where bone is.

mistakes.w: Wavefronts get further apart in glass.
mistakes.r: Wavefronts get **closer together** in glass because the wavelength is shorter at the lower speed.

exam.q: State two things that can happen to an electromagnetic wave when it meets a surface, other than being reflected.
model: absorbed (1)
transmitted / refracted (1)
exam.tip: Use the exact verbs: absorb, transmit, refract, reflect.

exam.q: Explain why a person can see the food inside a microwave oven through the metal mesh in the door, but the microwaves do not escape.
model: mesh reflects microwaves / microwaves cannot pass through the holes (1)
visible light has a much shorter wavelength so it is transmitted through the holes (1)
exam.tip: The key word is wavelength: the same mesh treats two wavelengths differently.

exam.q: X-ray images show bones clearly. Explain why.
model: bone absorbs X-rays (more than soft tissue) (1)
soft tissue transmits X-rays so the detector behind it is exposed, leaving bone as a contrasting shadow (1)
exam.tip: Contrast absorption by bone with transmission by soft tissue.

exam.q: Light travels from air into glass along the normal. Describe what happens to its speed, wavelength and direction.
model: speed decreases (1)
wavelength decreases (1)
direction does not change (1)
exam.tip: Along the normal there is no change of direction, but there is still refraction in the sense of a speed change.

exam.q: State what happens to the frequency of light when it passes from water into air.
model: it stays the same (1)
exam.tip: Frequency is set by the source.

exam.q: Light of frequency 5.0 x 10^14 Hz travels through water at 2.25 x 10^8 m/s. Calculate its wavelength in water.
exam.tip: Rearrange v = f x λ before substituting, and give the unit.

exam.q: (Higher) Explain, in terms of wavefronts, why light changes direction when it enters a glass block at an angle.
model: light travels more slowly in glass than in air (1)
one end/side of a wavefront reaches the glass first and slows down first (1)
the rest of the wavefront is still travelling faster in air, so the wavefront changes direction / pivots (1)
wavefronts are closer together in the glass / wave bends towards the normal (1)
exam.tip: Speed change first, then the unequal speeds across the wavefront, then the new direction.

exam.q: Explain why it is difficult to observe X-rays from distant stars using a telescope on the ground, but easy to observe visible light.
model: the atmosphere absorbs X-rays (1)
the atmosphere transmits visible light (1)
exam.tip: Same substance (air), different wavelengths, different effect.

exam.q: A beam of white light enters a triangular glass prism. Explain why a spectrum of colours is seen.
model: different colours have different wavelengths (1)
different wavelengths travel at different speeds in glass / are refracted by different amounts (1)
so the colours spread out; violet refracted most and red least (1)
exam.tip: Link the amount of refraction to wavelength.

exam.q: (Higher) Electromagnetic waves can be absorbed, transmitted, refracted or reflected by different substances. Discuss how these effects depend on the substance and on the wavelength of the radiation. Use examples from across the electromagnetic spectrum. Include an explanation of refraction in terms of speed.
model: effects vary with wavelength: the same substance behaves differently for different parts of the spectrum
glass transmits visible light but absorbs much ultraviolet
metal reflects microwaves/radio waves; water in food absorbs microwaves, so food heats up
bone absorbs X-rays while soft tissue transmits them; lead absorbs X-rays and gamma rays
atmosphere transmits visible light and radio but the ozone layer absorbs UV and X-rays are absorbed
refraction is caused by a change in speed at a boundary; slower in glass/water than air
one side of a wavefront slows first so the wave changes direction towards the normal; frequency is unchanged, wavelength decreases
exam.tip: Level 3 answers need examples for each effect AND a correct speed-based explanation of refraction, written as linked reasoning.

worked.q: Red light has a frequency of 4.6 x 10^14 Hz. Its speed in air is 3.0 x 10^8 m/s and in glass is 2.0 x 10^8 m/s. Calculate its wavelength in air and in glass, and state what happens to the frequency.
steps: Write the equation: v = f x λ, so λ = v / f.
In glass: the frequency is unchanged at 4.6 x 10^14 Hz.
Check: the speed fell to 2/3 of its value, so the wavelength should also be 2/3: 6.52 x 10^-7 x 2/3 = 4.35 x 10^-7 m. Consistent.
worked.ans: About 6.5 x 10^-7 m in air and 4.3 x 10^-7 m in glass; the frequency stays at 4.6 x 10^14 Hz.

worked.q: Light takes a time t to cross a glass window 6.0 mm thick at right angles. The speed of light in the glass is 2.0 x 10^8 m/s. Calculate t, and state whether the light changes direction.
steps: Convert thickness to metres: 6.0 mm = 6.0 x 10^-3 m.
time = distance / speed = 6.0 x 10^-3 / 2.0 x 10^8.
The light travels along the normal (at right angles to the surface), so although its speed changes it does not change direction.
worked.ans: t = 3.0 x 10^-11 s; no change of direction because it travels along the normal.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why a person gets less sunburnt sitting behind a closed glass window than sitting outside, even though the room is just as bright.
steps: Sunlight contains visible light and ultraviolet.
Glass transmits visible light, so the room is still bright.
Glass absorbs much of the ultraviolet, so less UV reaches the skin.
Sunburn is caused by ultraviolet, so less UV means less sunburn.
This shows a substance responding differently to different wavelengths.
worked.ans: Glass transmits visible light but absorbs much of the ultraviolet that causes sunburn, so the effect of glass depends on wavelength.

phy_edx.4.7.summary: Every object, at every temperature, **emits and absorbs** electromagnetic radiation; a hotter object emits radiation of **greater intensity** with its **peak at a shorter wavelength**. A body stays at a **constant temperature** only when the **average power it absorbs equals the average power it radiates**: if it absorbs more it warms up, and if it radiates more it cools down. The Earth's temperature is set by the same balance between incoming radiation from the Sun and infrared radiated into space, which is affected by **greenhouse gases, clouds, ice and land use**.

core.h: All bodies emit and absorb radiation
core.p: Spec point 5.15P: **all bodies (objects), no matter what temperature they are, emit and absorb infrared radiation** (thermal radiation). Even an ice cube emits infrared. What changes with temperature is **how much** radiation is emitted and **which wavelengths** it is spread across.
bullets: The particles in every object are always moving, and this motion causes the object to give out electromagnetic radiation.
At everyday temperatures the radiation is almost all **infrared**, which we cannot see but can feel as warmth.
Objects are also absorbing radiation from their surroundings all the time.
Whether an object warms up or cools down depends on the **balance** between the power it absorbs and the power it emits.
Thermal imaging cameras detect the infrared emitted by people, animals and buildings, even in the dark.

callouts.p: All bodies emit and absorb radiation at all temperatures. The intensity and distribution of the wavelengths of the radiation emitted depend on the temperature of the body.
Never say a cold object 'gives out cold' or 'does not radiate'. It emits infrared, just less than a hotter object.

core.p: A body emits a **continuous spread** of wavelengths, with a peak at one wavelength. As the body gets **hotter**, two things happen: the **total intensity** of the radiation increases, and the **peak shifts to shorter wavelengths**.
bullets: **Intensity** is the power per unit area, so a hotter body radiates more energy per second from each square metre.
A hotter body emits more at **every** wavelength, not just at the peak, so its curve sits above the cooler curves everywhere.
The **peak wavelength gets shorter** as temperature increases.
At a few hundred degrees Celsius the radiation is still mostly infrared; hotter still, enough visible light is emitted for the object to glow.
The Sun's surface is about 5500 degrees Celsius, so its peak is in the visible part of the spectrum.

fig.cap: Intensity against wavelength for bodies at three temperatures. The hottest body (5000 K) emits the most radiation at every wavelength, and its peak (dashed line) is at the shortest wavelength. As the temperature falls, the curve gets lower and its peak moves towards the infrared.

core.h: From red hot to white hot
core.p: The colour of a very hot object tells you about its temperature, because the distribution of wavelengths depends on temperature.
bullets: As a piece of metal is heated it first emits only infrared (you can feel it but not see it glow).
Hotter, it glows **dull red**, because the shortest wavelengths it now emits in useful amounts are at the red (long wavelength) end of the visible spectrum.
Hotter still it looks **orange, then yellow, then white**, as more and more shorter visible wavelengths are emitted.
**Stars** follow the same pattern: red stars are cooler, white and blue stars are hotter.
An electric heater element glowing red is cooler than a filament lamp glowing white.

core.p: When a body absorbs radiation, energy is transferred to its **thermal energy store**, so on its own absorption makes the temperature rise. How much a body absorbs depends on its **surface** as well as on how much radiation reaches it.
bullets: **Matt black** surfaces are the best absorbers **and** the best emitters of infrared.
**Shiny, silvery or white** surfaces are poor absorbers and poor emitters; they reflect most of the radiation.
A body in sunlight absorbs radiation from the Sun as well as from its surroundings.
The surface effect is investigated in core practical 5.19P (Leslie cube / cooling cans).

core.p: Spec point 5.16P: a body stays at a **constant temperature** when it **absorbs radiation at the same rate as it emits it**. In other words, the **average power absorbed equals the average power radiated**. It is still emitting and absorbing: the two simply cancel out.
bullets: Power is energy transferred per second, measured in **watts (W)**: 1 W = 1 J/s.
If power in = power out, there is **no net change** in the thermal energy store, so the temperature stays the same.
A cup of tea left long enough ends up at room temperature: then it absorbs from the room as much power as it radiates.
This is an example of a **dynamic equilibrium**: both processes continue at equal rates.

callouts.p: For a body to be at a constant temperature it needs to radiate the same average power that it absorbs.
At constant temperature the body has not stopped emitting or absorbing. Emission and absorption are both happening at the same rate.

core.p: Spec point 5.17P asks what happens if the average power radiated is **less** or **more** than the average power absorbed. The answer is always about the **net** transfer of energy to or from the body's thermal energy store.
bullets: **Absorbs more power than it radiates**: net energy is gained, the thermal energy store increases, so the **temperature rises**.
**Radiates more power than it absorbs**: net energy is lost, the thermal energy store decreases, so the **temperature falls**.
The bigger the difference between the powers, the faster the temperature changes.
Example: a parked car in strong sunlight absorbs more than it radiates, so it heats up.
Example: a hot pie taken out of the oven radiates more than it absorbs from the cooler kitchen, so it cools down.

core.p: A body that is warming does not warm up forever. As its temperature rises it **radiates more power** (a hotter body emits more intense radiation). Eventually the power radiated rises to equal the power absorbed, and the temperature stops changing at a **new, higher constant temperature**.
bullets: At first the gap between absorbed and radiated power is large, so the temperature rises quickly.
As the body heats up, radiated power increases, the gap shrinks, and the temperature rises more slowly.
When radiated power = absorbed power, the temperature levels off.
The same reasoning in reverse explains why a cooling body cools quickly at first and then more slowly.
On a temperature against time graph this gives a curve that levels off (gradient decreasing to zero).

callouts.p: Explain the levelling off using the idea that the emitted power depends on temperature. This is the step most students miss.

fig.cap: Temperature of an object placed in sunlight. It rises quickly at first while it absorbs much more power than it emits, then more slowly as its rising temperature makes it emit more. It levels off when emitted power equals absorbed power.

core.p: Spec point 5.18P: the **temperature of the Earth** depends on the balance between the **radiation it absorbs from the Sun** and the **radiation it emits into space**. If the two powers are equal, the Earth's average temperature stays constant.
bullets: The Sun is very hot, so most of its radiation is **visible light** and **shorter-wavelength infrared** (plus some ultraviolet).
Some incoming radiation is **reflected** straight back into space by clouds, ice, snow and other bright surfaces.
The rest is **absorbed** by the Earth's surface and atmosphere, warming them.
The Earth is much cooler than the Sun, so it emits **longer-wavelength infrared**.
Some of this infrared escapes into space; some is **absorbed by greenhouse gases** in the atmosphere.

fig.cap: The Earth's radiation balance. Radiation from the Sun is partly reflected by clouds and partly absorbed by the surface. The warm surface emits longer-wavelength infrared; some escapes to space and some is absorbed by greenhouse gases, which re-emit part of it back towards the ground.

core.p: **Greenhouse gases** such as **carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour** let most incoming short-wavelength radiation from the Sun pass through, but **absorb some of the longer-wavelength infrared** emitted by the Earth. They then **re-emit** infrared in all directions, including back down to the surface.
bullets: This means less power escapes into space than would without the gases.
The Earth warms until it radiates enough power to balance what it absorbs again, at a **higher equilibrium temperature**.
The natural greenhouse effect keeps the Earth's average surface temperature at about 15 degrees Celsius; without it the average would be well below freezing.
Burning fossil fuels and deforestation increase the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, strengthening the greenhouse effect.
The result is **global warming**: an increase in the Earth's average temperature.

callouts.p: Incoming radiation is mainly short wavelength (Sun is hot); outgoing radiation is long-wavelength infrared (Earth is cooler). Greenhouse gases absorb the long-wavelength infrared.

core.h: Factors that control the Earth's temperature
core.p: Anything that changes **how much radiation is absorbed** or **how much is emitted into space** changes the Earth's temperature. These are the factors you should be able to discuss.
bullets: **Greenhouse gas concentration**: more carbon dioxide, methane or water vapour means more outgoing infrared is absorbed, so less power is emitted to space and the temperature rises.
**Cloud cover**: clouds reflect incoming sunlight (cooling by day) but also absorb and re-emit outgoing infrared (keeping nights warmer).
**Ice and snow cover**: bright surfaces reflect more incoming radiation; melting ice exposes darker land or sea that absorbs more, which warms the Earth further.
**Land use**: forests, deserts, oceans and cities absorb and reflect different amounts of radiation.
**Output of the Sun**: more power from the Sun means more absorbed.
**Dust and ash** in the atmosphere (e.g. from large volcanic eruptions) can reflect sunlight and lower the temperature for a while.

core.p: Local temperature changes follow exactly the same rules. During the day the ground absorbs more power than it radiates, so it warms. At night there is no incoming sunlight, so the ground radiates more than it absorbs and cools.
bullets: **Clear nights** are colder because infrared from the ground escapes easily into space.
**Cloudy nights** are warmer because clouds absorb infrared from the ground and re-emit some back down.
**Cloudy days** are often cooler because clouds reflect a lot of incoming sunlight.
Frost is most likely on clear, still nights for this reason.

core.p: Questions on 5.15P to 5.18P reward clear chains of reasoning using the words **power**, **absorbed**, **radiated/emitted**, **balance** and **wavelength**.
bullets: For a temperature change, always compare **power absorbed** with **power radiated**.
For constant temperature, write 'average power absorbed = average power radiated'.
For graphs of intensity against wavelength: hotter means **higher curve** and **peak at shorter wavelength**.
For the Earth: incoming short-wavelength radiation, reflected or absorbed; outgoing long-wavelength infrared, escaping or absorbed by greenhouse gases.
In 6-mark questions, finish by linking the change back to the temperature of the Earth.

callouts.p: 'Absorbs more power than it emits' scores; 'gets more heat' usually does not.

analogy.t: A bath with the tap on and the plug out
analogy.p: Think of the body's thermal energy store as the water in a bath. The tap is the power absorbed and the plughole is the power radiated. If the tap runs faster than the drain, the water level (temperature) rises; if the drain wins, it falls; if they match, the level stays steady even though water is still flowing in and out. Even better, the deeper the water, the faster it drains, just as a hotter body radiates more power, so the level settles at a new steady height. Adding greenhouse gases is like partly blocking the plughole: the level rises until the extra pressure makes the drain flow match the tap again. Where it breaks down: water is a substance, but energy is not; and a real body's emitted power depends on its surface as well as its temperature.

terms.d: Infrared radiation emitted by an object because of its temperature.
To give out radiation.
To take in radiation, transferring its energy to the object's thermal energy store.
The power of radiation per unit area (W/m2).
The wavelength at which a body emits radiation with the greatest intensity; it is shorter for hotter bodies.
How the emitted radiation is spread across different wavelengths; it depends on temperature.
The rate of transfer of energy, in watts (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s.
The state in which a body absorbs radiation at the same average rate as it emits it, so its temperature is constant.
The energy a body has because of the motion of its particles; it increases when the temperature rises.
A gas such as carbon dioxide, methane or water vapour that absorbs longer-wavelength infrared emitted by the Earth and re-emits it.
The warming of the Earth because greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit outgoing infrared, so less power escapes into space.
The rise in the Earth's average temperature linked to increased greenhouse gas concentrations.
Radiation from the Sun sent straight back into space by clouds, ice, snow or bright surfaces without being absorbed.
Part of the electromagnetic spectrum with wavelengths longer than visible light; the main radiation emitted by objects at everyday temperatures.
A balance in which two opposite processes continue at equal rates, so there is no overall change.

mistakes.w: Cold objects do not emit radiation.
mistakes.r: **All bodies emit radiation at all temperatures**; cold ones emit less intense radiation at longer wavelengths.

mistakes.w: At constant temperature the object stops absorbing and emitting.
mistakes.r: It still absorbs and emits; the **average power absorbed equals the average power radiated**.

mistakes.w: A hotter object emits longer wavelengths.
mistakes.r: A hotter object's **peak wavelength is shorter**, and it emits more intensely at all wavelengths.

mistakes.w: The object heats up because it absorbs radiation.
mistakes.r: It heats up because it **absorbs more power than it radiates** (net gain of energy).

mistakes.w: Greenhouse gases trap the Sun's rays.
mistakes.r: Greenhouse gases **absorb the longer-wavelength infrared emitted by the Earth** and re-emit some back; most incoming short-wavelength radiation passes through.

mistakes.w: The greenhouse effect is caused by the hole in the ozone layer.
mistakes.r: The ozone layer absorbs UV; the greenhouse effect is about **infrared absorbed by greenhouse gases** such as carbon dioxide and methane.

mistakes.w: Clouds only make the Earth warmer.
mistakes.r: Clouds **reflect incoming sunlight** (cooling by day) as well as absorbing outgoing infrared (warming at night).

mistakes.w: The Earth emits the same type of radiation as the Sun.
mistakes.r: The Earth is much cooler, so it emits **longer-wavelength infrared**; the Sun emits mainly visible and short-wavelength infrared.

mistakes.w: When the object is hotter it will keep getting hotter while in the Sun.
mistakes.r: As its temperature rises it **radiates more power**, until radiated power equals absorbed power and the temperature becomes constant.

exam.q: State what is meant by the statement 'all bodies emit radiation'.
model: every object, at any temperature, gives out (infrared) radiation (1)
exam.tip: Include 'at all temperatures'.

exam.q: Describe how the radiation emitted by a body changes as its temperature increases.
model: intensity / total power emitted increases (1)
peak wavelength decreases / more shorter-wavelength radiation emitted (1)
exam.tip: Two separate changes: how much, and which wavelengths.

exam.q: A metal bar is heated in a flame. It glows red, then orange, then yellow-white. Explain this colour change.
model: as temperature increases the distribution of wavelengths changes (1)
peak moves to shorter wavelength (1)
so more of the shorter visible wavelengths (orange, yellow, blue) are emitted, making the colour change from red towards white (1)
exam.tip: Link colour to wavelength, and wavelength to temperature.

exam.q: A rock in a desert has a constant temperature during part of the afternoon. Explain why.
model: the rock absorbs radiation and emits radiation (1)
the average power absorbed equals the average power radiated (1)
exam.tip: Use the spec wording about average power.

exam.q: A cup of hot coffee is left in a room. Explain, in terms of radiation, why the coffee cools down and why it eventually stops cooling.
model: coffee radiates more power than it absorbs from the cooler room (1)
so there is a net loss of energy from its thermal energy store and temperature falls (1)
as it cools it radiates less power (1)
when it reaches room temperature, power radiated = power absorbed, so the temperature stays constant (1)
exam.tip: Explain both the cooling and the levelling off.

exam.q: A satellite in space absorbs 1200 W from the Sun and radiates 1500 W. State and explain what happens to its temperature.
model: temperature decreases (1)
because it radiates more power than it absorbs / net loss of 300 W (1)
exam.tip: Compare the two powers and give the net value if you can.

exam.q: Explain why the radiation emitted by the Earth has a longer wavelength than the radiation emitted by the Sun.
model: the Earth is much cooler than the Sun (1)
cooler bodies emit radiation with a peak at a longer wavelength (1)
exam.tip: Temperature controls the wavelength distribution.

exam.q: Explain why clear nights are usually colder than cloudy nights.
model: at night the ground radiates infrared and receives no sunlight (1)
on a clear night more infrared escapes into space (1)
clouds absorb infrared and re-emit some back to the ground, so less net energy is lost on a cloudy night (1)
exam.tip: Balance of power absorbed and radiated again.

exam.q: Explain how an increase in carbon dioxide in the atmosphere could lead to an increase in the average temperature of the Earth.
model: carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas that absorbs (longer-wavelength) infrared emitted by the Earth (1)
and re-emits some back towards the Earth (1)
so less power is radiated into space than is absorbed from the Sun (1)
so the Earth's temperature rises until a new balance is reached (1)
exam.tip: End with the balance idea, not just 'traps heat'.

exam.q: The temperature of the Earth depends on the balance between incoming radiation and radiation emitted. Discuss the factors that affect this balance and explain how each could change the Earth's temperature.
model: Earth's temperature is constant when average power absorbed = average power radiated
incoming radiation from the hot Sun is mainly short-wavelength; some reflected by clouds, ice and snow, the rest absorbed
Earth is cooler and emits longer-wavelength infrared
greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour) absorb outgoing infrared and re-emit some back, so less escapes
increasing greenhouse gases means more absorbed than radiated, so temperature rises until a new, higher balance
melting ice reduces reflection so more is absorbed, increasing temperature further
cloud cover reflects incoming radiation by day but absorbs outgoing infrared at night; volcanic dust can reflect sunlight and cool the Earth
exam.tip: Top-band answers name several factors and explain each through absorbed versus radiated power.

worked.q: An object absorbs radiation at a rate of 50 W and emits radiation at 35 W. (a) State what happens to its temperature. (b) Calculate the net energy gained in 2 minutes.
steps: (a) Power absorbed (50 W) is greater than power radiated (35 W), so there is a net gain of energy and the temperature rises.
(b) Net power = 50 - 35 = 15 W.
Time = 2 minutes = 120 s.
Energy = power x time = 15 x 120 = 1800 J.
worked.ans: (a) Temperature rises. (b) 1800 J (1.8 kJ) net energy gained.

worked.q: A thin metal plate is placed in sunlight. Describe and explain how its temperature changes over the next hour.
steps: At first the plate is at room temperature and absorbs more power from the Sun than it radiates.
So it gains energy and its temperature rises quickly.
As it gets hotter, it radiates more power (intensity of emitted radiation increases with temperature).
The difference between absorbed and radiated power gets smaller, so the temperature rises more slowly.
Eventually power radiated equals power absorbed, so the temperature stays constant.
worked.ans: The temperature rises quickly at first, then more slowly, then levels off when the plate radiates the same average power as it absorbs.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why melting of Arctic sea ice could cause further warming of the Earth.
steps: Ice and snow are bright surfaces that reflect a large fraction of incoming radiation from the Sun.
When the ice melts it exposes darker sea water, which absorbs more of the incoming radiation.
So the Earth absorbs more power while the power it radiates has not yet increased.
Absorbed power exceeds radiated power, so the Earth's temperature rises.
Higher temperature melts more ice, so the effect reinforces itself.
worked.ans: Less reflection and more absorption upsets the balance, so the Earth absorbs more power than it radiates and warms, melting more ice.

phy_edx.4.8.summary: In core practical 5.19P you investigate how the **colour and texture of a surface** affect how much **infrared (thermal) radiation** it emits or absorbs. Using a **Leslie cube** with an **infrared detector**, or identical cans of hot water with different coverings, you find that **matt black surfaces are the best emitters and absorbers**, while **shiny silver surfaces are the worst** because they reflect infrared. Exam questions test your method, **variables**, **safety**, ways to make the results **valid** (lids, equal volumes, same starting temperature, same distance) and how to **analyse cooling curves**.

core.h: What this core practical is about
core.p: Core practical 5.19P: **investigate how the nature of a surface affects the amount of thermal energy radiated or absorbed**. 'Nature of a surface' means its **colour** (black, white, silver) and its **texture** (matt/dull or shiny). The radiation involved is **infrared**.
bullets: You compare surfaces that are identical in every way except colour and texture.
To test **emission**, you start with identical hot objects with different surfaces and measure how fast they radiate (how fast they cool, or the infrared reading at a fixed distance).
To test **absorption**, you place different surfaces the same distance from a heater and see which warms up fastest.
This is a triple-only (Physics) practical and appears on Paper 1.

callouts.p: Investigate how the nature of a surface affects the amount of thermal energy radiated or absorbed.

core.p: **Matt black** surfaces are the **best emitters and the best absorbers** of infrared radiation. **Shiny silver (light, shiny)** surfaces are the **worst emitters and worst absorbers**, because they **reflect** most infrared. Matt white is in between.
bullets: A good absorber is always a good emitter; a poor absorber is always a poor emitter.
Dull (matt) surfaces emit and absorb more than shiny surfaces of the same colour.
Dark surfaces emit and absorb more than light surfaces of the same texture.
Ranking (best to worst emitter): **matt black, shiny black, matt white, shiny white / shiny silver**.
Good reflectors are poor absorbers: radiation that is reflected is not absorbed.

callouts.p: Matt black surfaces are the best emitters and absorbers of infrared; shiny silver surfaces are the worst and the best reflectors.

core.h: Method A: Leslie cube and infrared detector (emission)
core.p: A **Leslie cube** is a hollow metal cube with four different vertical faces, for example **matt black, shiny black, matt white and shiny silver**. It is filled with very hot water so all four faces are at the **same temperature**.
bullets: Place the Leslie cube on a heatproof mat and carefully fill it with hot water from a kettle (just boiled).
Put the lid on and wait a minute for the faces to reach the same temperature.
Place an **infrared detector** (or infrared thermometer) a fixed distance, e.g. 10 cm, from the centre of one face. Measure the distance with a ruler.
Record the reading, then turn the cube (or move the detector) to face each other surface at **exactly the same distance**.
Take the readings quickly, so the water does not cool much between readings, and repeat the set to check for consistency.
The face with the **highest reading** is the **best emitter**.

fig.cap: Leslie cube method. Hot water keeps all four faces at the same temperature. An infrared detector placed the same distance from each face measures how much infrared each surface emits; the matt black face gives the highest reading and the shiny silver face the lowest.

core.h: Method B: cooling cans or boiling tubes (emission)
core.p: Identical containers (cans, flasks or boiling tubes) are painted or wrapped so that each has a different surface. They are filled with the **same volume** of hot water at the **same starting temperature**, and the temperature of each is recorded as it cools.
bullets: Use containers of the same size, shape and material, so only the surface is different.
Wrap them in, for example, matt black paper, white paper and shiny aluminium foil.
Use a measuring cylinder to add **equal volumes** of hot water to each.
Fit each with a **lid** and a thermometer (or temperature probe) through the lid.
Record the starting temperature, then the temperature every minute (e.g. for 10 to 15 minutes).
Calculate the **temperature drop** for each container over the same time. The biggest drop shows the **best emitter**.

fig.cap: Cooling method. Three identical cans covered with different surfaces each hold the same volume of water at the same starting temperature, with a lid and a thermometer. The can whose temperature falls fastest has the surface that emits infrared best.

core.p: To compare **absorption**, the surfaces receive radiation from the same source. Two metal plates, one **matt black** and one **shiny**, are placed at **equal distances** either side of a radiant heater. A drawing pin is stuck to the back of each plate with a small blob of wax.
bullets: Switch on the heater; both plates receive the same infrared radiation.
The plate that absorbs more infrared heats up faster, melts its wax first and its **pin drops first**.
The pin on the **matt black** plate drops first, showing it is the **better absorber**.
Alternatively, place thermometers with differently painted bulbs, or identical cans of cold water, the same distance from a heater or lamp and record the temperature rise.
Use the same mass of wax and the same type of pin on each plate.

fig.cap: Absorption method. Two plates at equal distances from a radiant heater receive the same infrared radiation. Wax holds a pin on the back of each. The matt black plate absorbs more infrared, heats faster and its pin drops first.

core.p: In every version of this practical you change **only the surface** and keep everything else the same, so any difference in the results can only be caused by the surface.
bullets: **Independent variable**: the type of surface (colour and texture).
**Dependent variable**: the infrared detector reading, or the temperature drop (emission), or the temperature rise / time for the pin to drop (absorption).

**Control variables**: starting temperature of the water, volume of water, size, shape and material of the containers, distance from the detector or heater, time interval, room temperature, use of lids.

head: Variable type
Leslie cube
Cooling cans
rows: Temperature drop in a fixed time
Volume and starting temperature of water; lid; time

callouts.p: 'Keep it fair' scores nothing. Name the variable: 'the same volume of water' or 'the same distance from the detector'.

core.h: Making the results valid and accurate
core.p: Energy leaves the hot water by **conduction, convection and evaporation** as well as by radiation. Good technique keeps these other losses **the same for every container** (or reduces them) so that the difference is caused only by the radiation from the surface.
bullets: Use **lids** to reduce energy loss by evaporation and convection from the water surface.
Stand containers on the **same insulating mat** so conduction through the base is the same.
Keep containers well apart and away from draughts and windows, so they do not heat each other.
Start all containers at the **same temperature**, because hotter water cools faster.
**Stir** gently before reading so the thermometer reads the average temperature.
Read the thermometer at **eye level** to avoid **parallax error**.
Use **temperature probes and a data logger** to take readings at exactly the same times and with better resolution.
**Repeat** the experiment and calculate a mean to reduce the effect of **random errors**.

core.p: The main hazards in this practical are **hot water** and **hot surfaces**. You should be able to give a hazard and a precaution.
bullets: Hot water can **scald**: pour carefully, keep the kettle and containers on a stable bench, and do not move containers full of hot water.
Leslie cube faces get very hot: do not touch them; turn the cube using the handle or a cloth.
Radiant heaters get very hot: keep paper and hands away, and allow to cool before handling.
Mop up spills immediately to prevent slipping.
Do not pour water from a kettle while standing over the containers.

callouts.p: Always pair them: 'hot water could scald, so pour slowly and keep containers on a heatproof mat'.

core.p: For the cooling method, record time and temperature in a table for each surface, then plot **temperature (y-axis) against time (x-axis)** for all surfaces on the **same axes** with a smooth curve of best fit for each.
bullets: The **steepest curve** belongs to the **best emitter** (matt black).
Each curve gets **less steep over time**, because the water cools more slowly as it gets closer to room temperature.
Compare the **temperature drop** over the same time (e.g. 10 minutes) to put the surfaces in order.
Rate of cooling = temperature drop / time taken, in degrees Celsius per minute.
For the Leslie cube, a **bar chart** is used because the surface type is a **categoric** variable.

fig.cap: Typical cooling curves for identical cans of hot water. The matt black can cools fastest (steepest curve) because its surface emits infrared at the greatest rate. Both curves get less steep as the water gets closer to room temperature.

core.p: A good conclusion **describes the pattern** in the data and **explains it** using radiation ideas.
bullets: Pattern: the matt black surface gave the largest temperature drop / highest detector reading; shiny silver gave the smallest.
Explanation: the matt black surface **emits infrared radiation at a greater rate**, so energy is transferred away from the water faster.
Shiny surfaces **reflect** infrared back into the water and emit less.
For absorption: matt black **absorbs** more of the infrared falling on it, so it warms faster; shiny surfaces reflect most of it.
Only conclude about surfaces you actually tested, and comment on whether repeat readings were close (repeatable).

callouts.p: Quote numbers: 'the matt black can fell by 31 °C in 10 minutes but the shiny can by only 19 °C'.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to suggest why results were unreliable and how to improve the method.
bullets: **Different starting temperatures**: heat all the water together and pour at the same time, or start timing each can when it reaches the same temperature.
**Readings taken at slightly different times**: use data loggers.
**Leslie cube cooling during the readings**: take readings quickly, or refill with hot water and keep the time between readings short.
**Detector not at the same distance or angle**: clamp it and measure the distance with a ruler each time.
**Energy lost by convection/evaporation**: use lids and insulation underneath.
**Random error**: repeat and take a mean; identify and discard anomalous results.
**Systematic error**: check thermometers read the same in the same water before starting (zero/calibration check).

core.p: The result of this practical explains many designs. Examiners like you to apply it to new situations.
bullets: **Solar water heater panels** are matt black to absorb as much infrared as possible.
**Cooling fins** on the back of a fridge are often painted black to emit energy well.
**Emergency (space) blankets** are shiny to reduce emission from the body (and reflect radiation back).
**Houses in hot countries** are often painted white to reflect sunlight and absorb less.
**Teapots and vacuum flasks** with shiny surfaces lose less energy by radiation, keeping drinks hot longer.
Firefighters' suits are shiny to reflect infrared from fires.

core.h: Exam technique for the core practical
core.p: Questions on 5.19P test your ability to **describe a method**, name **variables**, explain **precautions**, process **data** and **evaluate**. A 6-mark method answer should be a clear sequence someone else could follow.
bullets: State the equipment, what you measure and with what (thermometer, infrared detector, stopwatch, ruler, measuring cylinder).
Say what you keep the same, with specific variables.
Describe how you would use the results to decide which surface is the best emitter or absorber.
Give at least one safety precaution linked to a hazard.
Link the conclusion to emission or absorption of **infrared radiation**, not just 'heat'.

analogy.p: Think of each surface as a doorway that infrared has to pass through. A matt black surface is a wide open doorway: energy passes out of a hot object easily (good emitter) and into a cold object easily (good absorber). A shiny silver surface is a doorway with a mirror across it: most radiation arriving from outside is bounced back (good reflector), and radiation from inside finds it hard to get out (poor emitter). Where it breaks down: a doorway suggests energy only leaves by radiation, but in the experiment energy is also lost by conduction, convection and evaporation, which is why lids and insulation are needed.

terms.d: Electromagnetic radiation emitted by all objects because of their temperature; the radiation measured in this practical.
A surface that gives out radiation; a good emitter gives out infrared at a high rate.
A surface that takes in radiation; a good absorber transfers most of the radiation falling on it to its thermal energy store.
A surface that sends most of the radiation falling on it back, rather than absorbing it.
A hollow metal cube with differently finished faces (e.g. matt black, shiny silver), filled with hot water so all faces are at the same temperature.
A device that measures the infrared radiation reaching it; a higher reading means more radiation.
A rough, non-shiny surface finish.
The variable you deliberately change: here, the type of surface.
The variable you measure: here, the temperature change or detector reading.
A variable kept the same so that it does not affect the results, e.g. volume of water or distance from the detector.
The temperature drop per unit time, e.g. in degrees Celsius per minute.
Unpredictable variation in readings, reduced by repeating and taking a mean.
An error that shifts all readings by the same amount, such as a thermometer that reads 1 degree too high.
An error caused by reading a scale from an angle rather than at eye level.
A variable described by names or labels (such as surface type), shown on a bar chart rather than a line graph.

mistakes.w: White surfaces are the best emitters because they are bright.
mistakes.r: **Matt black** surfaces are the best emitters and absorbers; white and shiny surfaces are poor emitters.

mistakes.w: Shiny surfaces absorb lots of infrared and then reflect it.
mistakes.r: Shiny surfaces **reflect** most infrared, so they **absorb little**.

mistakes.w: Good absorbers are poor emitters.
mistakes.r: A **good absorber is also a good emitter**; a poor absorber is a poor emitter.

mistakes.w: Control variable: keep it a fair test.
mistakes.r: Name a specific variable: **same volume of water, same starting temperature, same distance from the detector**.

mistakes.w: The black can cooled fastest because it lost more heat by conduction.
mistakes.r: It cooled fastest because the matt black surface **emits infrared radiation** at a greater rate.

mistakes.w: Dependent variable: the colour of the can.
mistakes.r: Colour/texture is the **independent** variable; the **temperature change or detector reading** is the dependent variable.

mistakes.w: Use a line graph to compare the Leslie cube faces.
mistakes.r: Surface type is **categoric**, so use a **bar chart**; line graphs are for temperature against time.

mistakes.w: Hazard: hot water. Precaution: be careful.
mistakes.r: Give a specific precaution: **pour slowly, keep containers on a stable heatproof mat, do not touch the hot cube**.

mistakes.w: Put the detector close to the cube for the black face to get a good reading.
mistakes.r: The detector must be the **same distance** from every face, or the comparison is invalid.

exam.q: State which surface is the best emitter of infrared radiation.
model: matt black (1)
exam.tip: Need both 'matt' and 'black' for the mark.

exam.q: In an experiment with a Leslie cube, state the independent variable and the dependent variable.
model: independent: type of surface / colour and texture of face (1)
dependent: reading on the infrared detector / amount of infrared radiation (1)
exam.tip: Independent is what you choose to change.

exam.q: Give two control variables for an experiment comparing how fast hot water cools in cans with different surfaces.
model: same volume of water (1)
same starting temperature / same size and material of can / same time interval / lids on all cans (1)
exam.tip: Be specific.

exam.q: Explain why the cans should all have lids.
model: lids reduce energy transfer by evaporation / convection from the water surface (1)
so the difference in cooling is caused by radiation from the surface only (1)
exam.tip: Link the precaution to validity.

exam.q: Explain why the infrared detector must be placed the same distance from each face of the Leslie cube.
model: the amount of radiation reaching the detector depends on its distance from the face (1)
so a fair comparison of surfaces needs equal distances / distance is a control variable (1)
exam.tip: Say why distance matters, not just that it must be kept the same.

exam.q: Describe one hazard in this practical and a precaution to reduce the risk.
model: hot water / hot cube could cause scalds or burns (1)
pour carefully / keep on a heatproof mat / do not touch the faces / handle using the handle (1)
exam.tip: Hazard and matching precaution.

exam.q: A student finds that the matt black can cooled from 80 °C to 52 °C in 10 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of cooling.
model: temperature drop = 80 - 52 = 28 °C (1)
rate = 28 / 10 = 2.8 °C per minute (1)
exam.tip: Rate = change divided by time, with unit.

exam.q: Explain why the matt black can cooled faster than the shiny silver can.
model: matt black is a better emitter of infrared radiation (1)
so energy is transferred from the water to the surroundings at a greater rate (1)
exam.tip: Use the word 'emitter' and mention infrared.

exam.q: Suggest two improvements to the cooling cans experiment to make the results more accurate or repeatable.
model: use temperature probes/data logger to record at the same times (1)
repeat and calculate a mean / insulate the base / ensure the same starting temperature (1)
exam.tip: Each improvement needs a reason if the question says explain.

exam.q: Describe an experiment to investigate how the nature of a surface affects the amount of thermal energy radiated. Include how you would make it a valid test and how you would use your results.
model: fill a Leslie cube (or identical cans with different surfaces) with hot water from a kettle
all faces at the same temperature / equal volumes of water at the same starting temperature
place an infrared detector the same distance (e.g. 10 cm) from each face and record the reading (or measure temperature every minute with a thermometer for 10 minutes)
control variables: distance, water temperature, size/material of containers, lids
repeat readings and calculate means
safety: hot water, use heatproof mat, do not touch faces
highest reading / biggest temperature drop shows the best emitter; expect matt black best and shiny silver worst
exam.tip: Write it in logical order: set-up, measurements, controls, safety, analysis.

worked.q: Use the results table (matt black: 80 to 49 °C, matt white: 80 to 57 °C, shiny silver: 80 to 61 °C in 10 minutes) to rank the surfaces as emitters and calculate the mean rate of cooling of each.
steps: Matt black: drop = 80 - 49 = 31 °C; rate = 31 / 10 = 3.1 °C per minute.
Matt white: drop = 80 - 57 = 23 °C; rate = 23 / 10 = 2.3 °C per minute.
Shiny silver: drop = 80 - 61 = 19 °C; rate = 19 / 10 = 1.9 °C per minute.
The largest temperature drop shows the fastest energy transfer by radiation.
Ranking from best to worst emitter: matt black, matt white, shiny silver.
worked.ans: Matt black 3.1 °C/min (best emitter), matt white 2.3 °C/min, shiny silver 1.9 °C/min (worst emitter).

worked.q: Leslie cube readings at 10 cm: matt black 42, shiny black 35, matt white 21, shiny silver 9 (arbitrary units). A student repeated the matt black reading and got 38. Suggest why it was lower and how to avoid this.
steps: The repeat was taken later, after the water in the cube had cooled.
A cooler surface emits less infrared, so the detector reading is lower.
To avoid this, take all readings quickly, refill with freshly boiled water, or keep the water at a constant temperature with a heater.
Also check the detector is at exactly the same distance each time.
worked.ans: The water had cooled, so the face emitted less infrared; take readings quickly at a constant water temperature and fixed distance.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why a solar panel for heating water is painted matt black, using the results of this practical.
steps: The practical shows matt black surfaces are the best absorbers of infrared radiation.
A solar panel needs to absorb as much radiation from the Sun as possible.
More radiation absorbed means more energy transferred to the water's thermal energy store.
So the water heats up more and faster than with a shiny or white surface, which would reflect much of the radiation.
worked.ans: Matt black is the best absorber, so it transfers the most energy from the Sun's radiation to the water.

phy_edx.4.9.summary: All electromagnetic waves transfer energy, and the **energy carried increases with frequency**, so the potential danger of an EM wave increases from radio waves to gamma rays. Low-frequency waves such as microwaves and infrared harm the body mainly by **heating** (internal heating of body cells, skin burns), while high-frequency ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are **ionising** and can damage or mutate the DNA in cells, leading to skin cancer, eye conditions and other cancers. Edexcel expects you to explain the frequency link and to match each named radiation to its harmful effect.

core.h: The big idea: danger increases with frequency
core.p: The EM spectrum runs from radio waves (lowest frequency, longest wavelength) to gamma rays (highest frequency, shortest wavelength). The **higher the frequency, the more energy the radiation transfers**, so the **potential danger increases with increasing frequency**.
bullets: Order of increasing frequency and danger: radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.
Higher frequency means shorter wavelength, because all EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum (v = f x wavelength).
Higher frequency radiation carries **more energy per packet (photon)**, so each packet can do more damage to a cell.
Above visible light (UV, X-rays, gamma) the radiation is **ionising**: it has enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms.
Below this (radio, microwave, infrared) the main hazard is **heating** of tissue.
How much harm is done also depends on the **dose**: intensity of the radiation and the length of exposure.

callouts.p: The potential danger associated with an electromagnetic wave increases with increasing frequency.

core.h: Why higher frequency is more dangerous
core.p: Energy transferred by an EM wave depends on its frequency. A high-frequency wave delivers its energy in larger packets, and a big enough packet can break chemical bonds or ionise atoms in a cell, which a low-frequency wave cannot do however long it shines.
bullets: **Higher frequency -> more energy transferred** -> more likely to damage cells.
Low-energy packets (radio, microwave, infrared) only make particles vibrate faster, raising temperature.
High-energy packets (UV, X-ray, gamma) can **ionise** atoms and **damage DNA**.
Damaged DNA can cause **mutations**; mutated cells may divide uncontrollably, which is **cancer**.
Very large doses can kill cells outright (radiation sickness, burns).

callouts.p: For an 'explain' question write the chain: higher frequency -> more energy -> can ionise / damage cells -> more dangerous.

core.p: Ionisation means removing electrons from atoms (or molecules) so they become charged ions. Ions are chemically reactive and can break or alter DNA molecules in the nucleus of a cell.
bullets: **Non-ionising**: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light: hazard is mainly heating.
**Ionising**: ultraviolet (higher frequency part), X-rays and gamma rays.
Gamma rays and X-rays are the most penetrating, so they can reach and damage cells **deep inside the body**.
UV is absorbed by the **outer layers of skin and by the eyes**, so it damages surface cells.

callouts.p: Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, turning them into ions.

fig.cap: A high-frequency X-ray or gamma photon transfers enough energy to knock an electron out of an atom, leaving a positive ion. Ionisation inside a cell can damage DNA and cause mutations.

core.h: Microwaves: internal heating of body cells
core.p: Microwaves are absorbed by water molecules and can **penetrate a few centimetres** into the body. Excessive exposure causes **internal heating of body cells**, which can damage or kill them.
bullets: Harmful effect named in the spec: **internal heating of body cells**.
Heating happens inside the body, not just at the surface, because microwaves pass through skin.
Microwave ovens have a metal case and a metal mesh in the door to keep microwaves inside.
Mobile phone microwaves are very low intensity; there is no confirmed evidence of harm at normal levels.

callouts.p: Microwaves do not cause cancer by ionisation. Their hazard is heating.

core.p: Infrared is absorbed by the skin and transfers energy to it as thermal energy. Too much infrared raises the temperature of skin cells enough to **burn** them.
bullets: Harmful effect named in the spec: **skin burns**.
Infrared is absorbed near the surface, so damage is to the skin.
Sources: fires, grills, heaters, very hot objects.
Protection: keep a safe distance, use heat-resistant gloves or shields.

core.p: Ultraviolet has a higher frequency than visible light and is ionising. It is absorbed by the surface layers of the skin and by the eyes, so it **damages surface cells and eyes, leading to skin cancer and eye conditions**.
bullets: Short term: **sunburn** (damage to surface skin cells).
Long term: **premature skin ageing** and **skin cancer** caused by DNA damage in skin cells.
Eyes: damage to the surface of the eye and **eye conditions such as cataracts**; can cause temporary blindness (snow blindness).
Sources: the Sun, sunbeds, UV lamps.
Protection: sunscreen (absorbs UV), clothing, hats, UV-blocking sunglasses, limiting time in strong sunlight or on sunbeds.

callouts.p: Ultraviolet: damage to surface cells and eyes, leading to skin cancer and eye conditions.

core.h: X-rays and gamma rays: mutation or damage to cells
core.p: X-rays and gamma rays have the highest frequencies. They are strongly ionising and **highly penetrating**, passing into and through the body. Excessive exposure causes **mutation or damage to cells in the body**.
bullets: Ionisation damages DNA -> **mutations** -> can lead to **cancer**.
High doses **kill cells** (this is used deliberately in radiotherapy to kill cancer cells).
Because they penetrate, they can damage **internal organs**, not just the skin.
Rapidly dividing cells (e.g. in a developing baby) are especially at risk.

callouts.p: Write 'mutation or damage to cells in the body', not just 'it is bad for you' or 'radiation poisoning'.

bullets: Radio and visible light are not on the spec's hazard list; their risk at normal levels is low.
Effects from microwaves and infrared come from **heating**; effects from UV, X-rays and gamma come from **ionisation**.

core.p: 'Excessive exposure' is the key phrase. Risk depends on how much radiation energy the body absorbs, which depends on the **intensity** of the source and the **duration** of exposure, as well as the frequency.
bullets: Brief, low-intensity exposure (e.g. one medical X-ray) gives a small risk.
Repeated or long exposure increases the risk of harm.
Distance from the source reduces intensity, so standing further away reduces dose.
Shielding (lead for X-rays and gamma, sunscreen for UV) reduces the energy reaching cells.

callouts.p: Exam questions often ask whether a use is justified. Weigh the benefit (e.g. diagnosis) against the small risk from a low dose.

core.p: Workers who use EM radiation regularly receive many small doses, so they are protected more carefully than patients who receive one dose.
bullets: Radiographers stand **behind a lead screen** or leave the room during an X-ray.
Workers wear **lead aprons** and badges (dosimeters) that record exposure.
Patients have the dose kept as low as possible and other body parts shielded.
Sunscreen, sunglasses and covering skin reduce UV exposure.
Microwave ovens are shielded with a metal case and door mesh.

core.h: Comparing two radiations in an exam answer
core.p: When asked which of two radiations is more dangerous, compare frequency first, then link to energy and effect.
bullets: State which has the **higher frequency** (or shorter wavelength).
Say it **transfers more energy**.
Name the effect: e.g. ionising, can damage DNA / cause mutation / cancer.
Mention penetration if relevant: gamma reaches internal organs, UV only surface cells.

callouts.p: Danger increases with frequency, so danger DEcreases with increasing wavelength. Do not say 'longer wavelength is more dangerous'.

analogy.p: Low-frequency radiation is like a steady stream of soft sponge balls: lots of them warm the glass but none can crack it (heating only). High-frequency radiation is like throwing steel ball bearings: each one carries enough energy to crack the glass on its own (ionisation, DNA damage). More balls (higher intensity) or longer throwing (longer exposure) make damage more likely. It breaks down because a huge number of sponge balls still never crack the glass, whereas very intense infrared or microwaves can still burn or cook tissue; also real radiation is not a lump that bounces off but energy that is absorbed.

terms.d: The continuous range of EM waves ordered by frequency: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.
The number of waves passing a point per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
The distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave, in metres.
The likelihood and severity of harm from exposure; for EM waves it increases with frequency.
Receiving more radiation (higher intensity or longer time) than is safe.
Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms to form ions; includes UV, X-rays and gamma rays.
An atom or molecule that has gained or lost electrons and so is charged.
A change in the DNA of a cell, which may cause the cell to behave abnormally.
A disease in which mutated cells divide uncontrollably.
Heating of body cells from the inside, caused by excessive microwave exposure.
Damage to skin from overheating, caused by excessive infrared exposure.
Damage to the eyes, such as cataracts, caused by excessive ultraviolet exposure.
Able to pass into or through materials such as body tissue; X-rays and gamma rays are highly penetrating.
The amount of radiation energy absorbed by the body, which depends on intensity and duration of exposure.
Lead screens or aprons that absorb X-rays and gamma rays to protect workers.

mistakes.w: Longer wavelength radiation is more dangerous.
mistakes.r: Danger increases with **frequency**; higher frequency means shorter wavelength, so shorter wavelengths are more dangerous.

mistakes.w: Microwaves cause cancer by ionising cells.
mistakes.r: Microwaves cause **internal heating of body cells**; they are not ionising.

mistakes.w: Infrared causes skin cancer.
mistakes.r: Infrared causes **skin burns**; ultraviolet causes skin cancer.

mistakes.w: UV is dangerous because it goes deep into the body.
mistakes.r: UV damages **surface cells and eyes**; it is absorbed by the outer layers.

mistakes.w: Gamma rays are dangerous because they are hot.
mistakes.r: Gamma rays are dangerous because they are **ionising** and cause **mutation or damage to cells**.

mistakes.w: Higher frequency waves travel faster so hit harder.
mistakes.r: All EM waves travel at the **same speed in a vacuum**; higher frequency waves transfer **more energy**.

mistakes.w: X-rays cause sunburn.
mistakes.r: Sunburn is from UV; X-rays cause **mutation or damage to cells in the body**.

mistakes.w: Radiation is dangerous because it is radioactive.
mistakes.r: EM radiation is not radioactive material; it transfers energy, and high-frequency radiation can ionise atoms.

exam.q: State how the potential danger of an electromagnetic wave changes as its frequency increases.
model: Danger increases (as frequency increases).
exam.tip: One word answers like 'increases' are fine for 1 mark, but name what increases.

exam.q: Name the type of electromagnetic radiation that can cause skin burns.
model: Infrared.
exam.tip: Do not say UV: sunburn is UV but 'skin burns' in the spec list is infrared.

exam.q: Describe the harmful effect of excessive exposure to microwaves.
model: Internal heating of body cells.
exam.tip: Use the word 'internal'.

exam.q: Give two harmful effects of excessive exposure to ultraviolet radiation.
model: Damage to surface cells / sunburn / skin cancer.
Damage to eyes / eye conditions / cataracts.
exam.tip: Give one skin effect and one eye effect for both marks.

exam.q: Explain why gamma rays are more dangerous than infrared radiation.
model: Gamma rays have a higher frequency (so transfer more energy).
Gamma rays are ionising / can cause mutation or damage to cells (infrared only heats).
exam.tip: Always state the frequency comparison first.

exam.q: X-rays and gamma rays can damage cells deep inside the body but ultraviolet mainly damages the skin. Explain why.
model: X-rays and gamma rays are (highly) penetrating / pass through tissue.
UV is absorbed by the surface layers of skin (and eyes).
exam.tip: Penetration explains where the damage happens; frequency explains how much.

exam.q: A radiographer takes many X-ray images each day. Explain why she stands behind a lead screen even though patients do not.
model: She is exposed many times so her total dose would be large / risk builds up.
Lead absorbs X-rays, reducing her exposure (and so risk of mutation / cancer).
exam.tip: Mention repeated exposure, not just 'X-rays are dangerous'.

exam.q: Sunscreen absorbs ultraviolet radiation. Explain how using sunscreen reduces the risk of skin cancer.
model: Less UV reaches the skin cells.
Less damage to (DNA in) surface cells so fewer mutations that could cause cancer.
exam.tip: Link the absorption to reduced cell damage.

exam.q: Describe the harmful effects of excessive exposure to X-rays and gamma rays.
model: They can cause mutation (of DNA) in cells (leading to cancer).
They can damage or kill cells in the body.
exam.tip: Spec wording: mutation or damage to cells in the body.

exam.q: Explain why the potential danger associated with electromagnetic waves increases with frequency. Refer to named regions of the spectrum in your answer.
model: Higher frequency EM waves transfer more energy.
Low frequency waves such as microwaves and infrared cause heating (internal heating / skin burns).
Higher frequency waves such as UV, X-rays and gamma rays are ionising.
Ionisation can damage DNA / cause mutations / cancer, which is more serious.
exam.tip: Name at least one low and one high frequency example.

exam.q: Discuss the harmful effects on people of excessive exposure to different types of electromagnetic radiation, and explain how the hazard is related to frequency.
model: Danger increases with increasing frequency because higher frequency waves transfer more energy.
Microwaves cause internal heating of body cells.
Infrared causes skin burns.
Ultraviolet damages surface cells and eyes, leading to skin cancer and eye conditions.
X-rays and gamma rays cause mutation or damage to cells in the body.
UV, X-rays and gamma are ionising; X-rays and gamma are penetrating so affect internal organs; risk also depends on intensity and length of exposure.
exam.tip: Work through the spectrum in order of frequency: it shows the trend and keeps the answer organised.

worked.q: Radiation A has a frequency of 3 x 10^10 Hz and radiation B has a frequency of 3 x 10^18 Hz. Identify each and state which is more hazardous and its harmful effect.
steps: 3 x 10^10 Hz lies in the microwave region (about 10^9 to 10^11 Hz).
3 x 10^18 Hz lies in the X-ray / gamma region.
B has the higher frequency, so it transfers more energy per photon.
B is ionising and can cause mutation or damage to cells in the body; A causes only internal heating.
worked.ans: A is microwaves, B is X-rays (or gamma). B is more hazardous: it can cause mutation or damage to cells, while A causes internal heating of body cells.

worked.q: A student says: 'A sunbed is safer than an X-ray because the X-ray only lasts a fraction of a second.' Evaluate this statement.
steps: X-rays have a higher frequency than UV, so each exposure carries more energy and they are more penetrating.
But risk also depends on dose: intensity and length of exposure.
A sunbed gives many minutes of UV exposure, repeated over many sessions, raising the risk of damage to surface cells and eyes, skin cancer and eye conditions.
A single medical X-ray gives a small, controlled dose, with the benefit of diagnosis.
worked.ans: Partly wrong: X-rays are more dangerous per exposure because of higher frequency, but repeated long sunbed use can give a large total UV dose, so frequent sunbed use may carry a greater overall risk of skin cancer than an occasional X-ray.
